en: The Great Poem of Śrī Hammīra, First Canto:
We worship that Supreme Light, the sole cause of the great arising of eternal consciousness and bliss.
In whom the glory of Śiva delights, as a female swan does in a lake of pure, transformative waters. ||1||

May that Nābhibhū, who is the abode of Lakṣmī, who brought about the end of worldly existence, and whom the virtuous—intent upon the knowledge and realization of Him—declare to be composed of the Supreme Brahman, grant you auspiciousness. 2.

May Śrīpārśva—the Supreme Person, whose auspicious activities were expanded by Yaśodā, whose lotus feet were worshipped by a garland of cowherds, and who bears the Śrīvatsa mark—bestow upon you vast and boundless prosperity. (3)

May the illustrious Śaṅkara, the heroic Lord, bring about prosperity—he who is the lofty bull, the destroyer of the pride of Kāma, followed by Pārvatī, resplendent with divine power, and who has dispelled the darkness through his pure abiding state. 4.

May the radiant Sun, who brings peace, possessing a magnificent splendor that delights the hearts of all who bear the wheel [of dharma], being ever-blessed and capable of fully manifesting perfect awakening, pacify all evils. 5.

May he whose feet are kissed by the crest-jewel of Maheśa, who stands unswerving, whose auspicious activity is vast, who has utterly destroyed the mass of great darkness, and who was born from the ocean—may he be for the glory of the moon! 6.

May Sarasvatī, who bestows great devotion through her radiant poetry, who is ever-gracious with the wealth of her lotus-like speech, and who purifies the three worlds by her very sight, lead us to her favor. (7)
How many lords of the earth were there not on this world, chief among whom were Mādhātṛ, Sītāpati, and Kaṅka?
Yet among them, O Hammīra, this one lord alone is worthy of praise for his supreme quality of courage. (8)

For him whose every movement was solely for the sake of sentient beings, did even the splendors of sovereignty and his very life become as insignificant as a blade of grass when he gave away his daughter to the Śaka king and granted protection to those who had sought refuge? (9)

In this great poem on the illustrious Hammīra, I desire to recount a portion of his life out of a wish to honor him as a king; for, impelled by the weight of his various noble qualities, have I not indeed been led to the very root of his ears? (10)
Where is the exceedingly great life-story of this king, and where is my intellect, so meager in comparison?
Yet, deluded by extreme infatuation, I desire to cross the great ocean with the aid of a single arm alone. (11)
If, by the grace of my Guru, I am indeed capable of composing a hymn to his life, does not the deer sport playfully in the sky through its association with the ripples of the moon? 12.
The sovereign Hammīra was the crest-jewel upon the crown of the illustrious Cāhamāna lineage;
I shall now relate his ancient origin, which generates a playful surge of joy. (13)
It is said that in the beginning, as the Creator was wandering about to find a meritorious spot for a sacrifice,
the Puṣkara lake suddenly fell from his lotus-hand, as if overcome by the radiance of his hand.
Then, having contemplated this auspicious place and having cast aside his dejection by commencing the sacrifice,
he— fearing danger from the hosts of demons— remembered the thousand-rayed Sun, who smiles with joy.
Then, from the circle of light of the Lord of Radiance, a man descended with a raised sword;
having consecrated him, he easily performed the sacrifice for the sake of protecting his horse.
Because a lotus (puṣkara) fell from Annapāṇi, this became known as Puṣkaratīrtha; and because that man who was called Āhāmana arrived here, it was therefore named Āhāmana. ||17||
Then, having attained imperial sovereignty through the grace born of the Four-faced One (Brahmā), that Dhāhamāna,
like the sun, swiftly overran the mountains— both those who were his elders and even his own fathers.
Beholding his generosity, which eclipsed the vast glory born of his own gifts, Bali took refuge in the cavern of the netherworld; for what other resort is there for those overcome by shame? (19)
O you sinner! You desire my fame, because of which the Moon, being obstructed by anger, enters the divine orb of the Sun every month and emerges only after bestowing his light. 20.
The fire of his majesty blazed forth and utterly consumed the forests of his enemies' fame;
because it took refuge in the smoke rising from that conflagration, the sky has not shed its blackness even to this day.
Having heard his fame, which was delightful due to its wonderful and noble conduct, Śeṣa— his mind filled with great joy—
shook his head out of fear that the surface of the earth would collapse, thereby causing the ocean to overflow.
Describing his ancestors:

He who, while fighting, caused the hosts of enemies—who had already suffered great separation from the goddess of victory—to faint completely; yet, though he acted like the wind, it is a marvel that he did not bring comfort even to the double-tongued serpents. 23.

"Does the son not indeed rival his father's fame, saying 'I am the moon'? Out of indignation at this, did the ocean not seize the very goddess of profundity from him? For is there no punishment for a father when his son commits an offense? (24)

Then, by that name, there arose a lineage of men praised throughout the three worlds—a lineage constantly served by rows of gods and serving as the source of origin for the pearls of human beings. (25)

In that lineage, which was a circle of flashing valor, there arose many kings whose burden of sin was terrified away by their wondrous deeds, purified by their engagement in the three aims of life (trivarga). ||26||
King Bhava, having pervaded the world with his valor, was initiated as Vāsudeva;
he descended here to earth like Vāsudeva himself to conquer the Śakas and Asuras. (27)
He who, having heated his sword— which was blunter than the edge of the skull of a host of rivals—
within the fire of his own majesty, caused the tears from the eyes of their beloved wives to drink it to satiety.

On the battlefield, the Goddess of Victory appeared intensely manifest in his hand under the guise of his sword-blade, which was smeared with the flood of blood from the roots of the heads of the severed circles of his enemies, as if she were clearly filled with passion for him. ||29||
While the multitude of battle-instruments resounded and the gods from heaven looked on,
he displayed the splendor of his heroism upon the field of battle by means of the brandishing of his flashing sword.
Since the sun, conquered by its brilliance, still leaps today into the ocean, why does it not emerge every day agitated?
Alas! This wretched life is so difficult to abandon. (31)

Then was born from his body King Śrī Naradeva, who was skilled in honoring those of noble birth, and whose physical beauty, so enchanting to the eyes of slender-waisted women, rivaled the form of the God of Love. (32)
When that king roamed about in a rage to ensure this entire world was free of enemies, his adversaries,
fearing for their royal fortune, drew wealth from their own treasuries rather than swords from their scabbards.

His arm, which bore the splendor of the peak of the eastern mountain at the beginning of the cosmic cycles, shone forth as it brought witheredness to the lotus-faces of his enemies; upon that arm, the gleam of a fresh crescent moon was resplendent. (34)
It was only fitting that his blazing fire of valor consumed the forests of injustice;
yet it is a marvel to the world that it spread such a weight of trembling among his enemies. (35)
In the great poem *Śrīhammīra*, [it is said]:
"Though accompanied by sons and grandsons, this lord of the twice-born was defeated by me through the guise of my fingernails;
'this is my fame,' saying this, he fell upon her pair of lotus-feet. (36)
Then, having acquired the earth through his singular statesmanship, King Śrīcandra caused it to bear the likeness of the moon;
by means of his face and his fame, he twice surpassed the maker of night, making his own name truly significant.
Of that blazing fire of his majesty, a certain unprecedented form arose:
it burned intensely against an enemy who was full of sap, yet it was instantly extinguished in this one who is sapless. (38)
Desirous of discharging volleys of arrows in battle, he drew the string of his bow;
that he swiftly sent his enemies to the abode of King Yama was not at all surprising. (39)
Between that lord of the earth and the Great Sage, there existed a very great mutual opposition:
one was dispassionate toward the wives of others, while the other was full of passion for them. (40)

Therefore, the most illustrious Mahendra, whose power was greatest and who bore the name Jayapāla, attained renown throughout the world as one perfected in knowledge, having conquered the circle of his enemies with the wheel of his majesty. (41)

In battle, the creeper-like sword of him whose splendor was like a fire of valor shone intensely, crimson with the blood gushing from the frontal globes of the temples of elephants that had been split by his blade. (42)

Skilled in bestowing the essence of many *aṣṭāpada* dice, having brought his own senses under control, he was known to others as a gambler who was unsurpassed in the games of battle with the four high-ranking divisions of the army. (43)

Upon his hand, the creeper-like sword shone like a pearl necklace of the Goddess of Victory, under the guise of pearls clinging to the frontal globes of the lordly elephants of his enemies that he had torn asunder. (44)

When the three worlds were completely surrounded on all sides by the floods of his fame, the wise reflected thus: "Surely this world has been heated by his splendors and then anointed with the sandalwood of his majesty. (45)
Having perceived her own splendor entirely eclipsed on all sides by his fame, does the celestial river even now not cry out loudly under the guise of the sound of her falling current? (46)
In battle, having drunk the honey-like blood from the lotus-faces of his enemies, the arrows of this king, like intoxicated bees, used to fall upon the surface of the earth from every side. (47)

When his spreading poison became a weapon, the sweat, trembling, and great loss of strength that arose in his adversaries who had encountered him in battle were like those of wives for their beloveds.

With a radiant fortitude, having attained brilliant renown, possessing pure complexion and admirable conduct, he— recollecting his former fame like a great poet— never directed his mind toward the destruction of another's welfare. (49)
Out of fear that "no one here shall know me because of my dwelling in opposition," it is said that fire entered the wood through his majesty;
otherwise, how could its origin be from the friction of that wood? (50)
Granted that some extraordinary vigor was produced even by the Creator;
yet it manifested as a certain breaking out of sweat, by which, spreading like a river, the water of even the ocean was rendered salty.

He established the fortress of Ajayameru—a site whose foundation was praised by the Creator upon beholding the overwhelming mass of the finest treasures of various riches, and which was beautiful with a luster that surpassed the splendors of heaven. (52)
Therefore, the king Jñānarāja was kindled, he whose very form was world-renowned fame;
by the moons of his glory, the faces of the women of the quarters became fragrant. (53)
When the cool-rayed moon was not perceived as distinct while his spreading fame shone forth,
I then suspected that the Creator had fashioned that spot within his orb as a screen for it.
While he ruled the earth, transgressing the royal highway was seen only in lofty temples;
cruelty resided only in weapons; intoxication only in elephants; and the seizing of the hand (taxes) appeared only in the act of marriage.
When the sun fell like a moth into the majesty of this lamp of the world, how else could the lords of poets have conceived for him the name "Pataṅga" (the Moth)? 56.
It is indeed true that even those born from the same womb or known under the same constellation may not be alike;
for though he was born at the same time as the sun, his vigor was scorching while his fame was cool.
Then there shone King Sāmantasiṃha, a lion among men and a lion amidst a host of rutting elephants;
by his majesties, the circle of enemies was conquered, and thus his sword-blade became a mere ornament. (58)

Oh, how the moon of his fame shone with ever-new splendor day and night—its great rising glory such that it was neither terrified by the lioness of adversity, nor did it possess the dull luster of a cloud-like enemy! 59.
His majesty, like the newly risen sun, shone indeed as it spread over the heads of the kings;
it scorched his enemies when they held their parasols, but never when they had laid aside their parasols.
His fame, as if out of anger, seems to vie with Indra, thinking, "He protects me alone, excluding the two [Indra and Agni]."
Clinging to his matted locks under the guise of the river Svastanī, she ascended the crown of the one who bears the moon upon his head.

The herds of deer speak of the sin of one who desires to compete in battle with those whose intellects are eclipsed by their own lack of discrimination— those who, like beasts, carry grass in their teeth.
Then, the lord of infinite subjects, named Gūyaka, enjoyed the splendor of sovereignty;
by him the tree of Dharma on earth was constantly sprinkled with the waters of liberality.
Beholding the sword-cloud raised within his hand, with its mass of water-drops in the form of unrestrained streams,
the pride-swans of his enemies fled even from Lake Mānasa upon seeing it.
Uttering the names of his enemy’s cattle as if they were blades of grass, holding a sword for a staff in his hand,
and with his entire body adorned without interruption, he who truly exercised the role of a cowherd.
Drinking up, drop by drop, the waters of the fame of his prostrate enemy kings,
his sword-blade— fanned by the breezes of the sighs of their women— acted like a serpent.
O descendant of Nanda, that king named Nandana, who brought joy to the people like sandalwood,
having slain all his enemies in battle, made this earth as far as the ocean his own.

By his mere presence, he caused auspicious things to flourish for men, and by his vision of the true nature of reality, he dispelled the darkness; like the sun, he who was delightful in his conduct continuously caused all beings to prosper.

Who indeed does not say that he was even more partial toward his enemies than toward his own side? For just as he never turned his back in battle, so too did his enemies never turn their faces away from him.
Having abandoned partiality toward his own side before his enemies, who indeed has said more of him than this:
that just as he drew his sword from its sheath, so too did he draw wealth from even his foes in battle? (70)
Has he entered the ascetic groves on the shores of the ocean to wipe away that sin which the world’s fire of his majesty, surpassing even the submarine fire, has produced by its mere touch? (71)

With his long arms extended out of fear and distress, a treasury for the secret doctrines of all the sciences of weaponry, and having effortlessly defeated the king of the gods, that monarch then [encircled] the king of ramparts with silver. || 72 ||

The glory of victory belonging to those who enjoy the lands of their adversaries—once scorched by the heat of the sun and the flames of their prowess—performed the graceful sport of immersion upon the falling of the sharp edge of his sword. (73)

If there were any similarity between this crawling serpent and my sword-blade in its mere outward form, then let it take away the host of lives only after biting; whereas we, the supreme among enemies, shall do so by the mere act of being seen.
Since his splendor surpasses all others, and his vigor and fame were intended by the Creator to be such,
these two— the sun of fierce radiance and the moon of cool rays— must surely have been fashioned for the sake of his praiseworthy emulation.

I suspect that his fame, for the sake of pacifying the sin of eclipsing the glory of every other king, repeatedly performs its ablutions in the current of the celestial river; otherwise, how could it possess such whiteness? (76)
Even though he had cast off all faults, two defects remained in him: subjection to passion and greed;
for he enjoyed the maiden army in battle, and likewise alone he seized the glory of victory.

Hearing the song of his fame, I suspect that Hara began to dance with spreading joy, appearing as white as if drenched by the streams of water from the celestial river flowing forth from his loosened matted locks. (78)

Though many beggars were clamoring about him, he who delighted solely in the sport of giving never favored any other than that syllable "Na" which follows the word "Dā"—if indeed that "Na" was dear to him. 79.
She is the wish-fulfilling creeper for those with no small resolve, a bhallī-arrow that pierces the multitude of opposing factions,
her feet worshipped by the rows of beings in the three worlds, and she who bestows great grace upon those intent on her service.
Having propitiated the goddess named Śākaṃbharī, who has made her abode at the site of Śākaṃbharī, the Lord of the Universe revealed Ruma at Śākaṃbharī for the welfare of the world. (81)
Then King Harirāja, who had conquered the circle of his enemies, took upon himself the burden of the earth;
having slain the sovereign of the Śakas in battle, he seized the city of Mugdha with great honor. (89)
On the field of battle, even a single warrior among those bearing enmity shone as if he were many,
appearing like the moon to the people who gazed upon him in vessels filled with clear water.
Having wandered through vast mountains yet finding no suitable union anywhere, virtues such as generosity and the like dwell day and night in his city, like citizens. (84)
"Is there any point in us studying these syllables in vain, or rather, is there a specific purpose?
For in this matter, the deliberation of the poets' speech is this: that we are forbidden from entering, yet we enter precisely to forbid. (85)
That this ocean of the sword of the generous [king] possesses such great unfathomable depth—what wonder is that to us?
But this is a marvel even among marvels:
that despite its being full of water, its dullness (or stupidity) does not manifest at all. 86.
The lords of boars, tortoises, and serpents support the earth with thousands of tusks, backs, hoods, and coils;
but what wonder does that not inspire in us when he supports it with ease upon a single arm? (87)

Then, from him was born Śrī Siṃharāja, who possessed the nature of a lord of the forest-dwellers; he took his seat upon his own throne, and with his mane shining under the guise of the pair of beautiful chowries waved by the wives of the multitude of powerful enemies—who had been utterly defeated by his valorous exertion—he became like a lion with a lofty gait and stride. (88)
When these [enemies], whose wicked fame was spreading,
had been terrified by this [king] and had fled from all sides onto the battlefield— which resembled a mass of flashing rain-clouds—
is it not fitting that the swans of their pride have now departed for good? For such is the nature of this [pride].
Or rather, it was set in motion by the embraces of their wives, who were distressed by separation. || 89 ||
How could the ocean of salt water, though possessing a dark luster, have given birth to him who is white-rayed and composed of nectar? For a son is indeed equal to his father;
yet today, O King, there is nothing superior to him, whose fame spreads abroad.
This ocean has been nourished by nectars; may you and your parents become like that. (90)

Lakṣmī, having drawn away from me the state of being the object of enjoyment that belonged to another, out of affection extends it to me; yet, though she is devoted to the vow of a single husband even beyond [the duty toward] her own progenitor,
when praised by poets, she distances herself from me and has no desire to hear me.
The fame of him whose [fame] has reached the heights has, as it were, become enraged and descended upon the territory of his adversaries.
While Bāṇa’s arrow and Indra’s sword were both held in his hand, this was a wonder of two kinds:
one [the sword] rushed forward in battle for the sake of the enemy target.
The forest, as it were, cast his own treasury far away. || 92 ||
In my view, the Creator has certainly not fulfilled his purpose after separating the unfathomable ocean and the Sumeru mountain— which is the very essence of supreme weight;
for having fashioned these two, the Blessed One has surely made them one again within this [body].
He was so delighted by [her] creation that he did not suffer as much in the act of creating her as he did in bringing her forth.
As if captivated by his beauty, the maiden Vijayaśrī abandoned all the other princes— who seemed scorched by misfortune— in the midst of battle;
she approached him to marry him, yet even upon touching his palm, she immediately became a mere radiance.
She gave birth to a son, the offspring of Kīrti; this is a great marvel in the world. || 94 ||
In an instant, the Karṇāṭa became a mere revealer of the forest of his own ears; the Lāṭa became a provider of door-panels;
the Śaulika had his heart trembling with terror for his weapons; the Gurjara became shattered and worn out;
and the Aṅga became one whose mind was bent upon the stage of battle.
Which, as the sound of the marching drum spreads forth, fills the belly of the quarters of space. || 95 ||
"O Sage Ocean, I have been surpassed by this mountain in terms of profundity;
do not, therefore, indulge in vain distress. Indeed, upon seeing one person, another should offer consolation.
Behold, O Lord, how this mountain stands firm through its capacity to support all beings and its loftiness."
He conquered [the world] in such a way that [his enemies], abandoning the path of their eyes, departed from his range of vision.
Just as he desired to place the gleaming bow in his hand,
the enemy king suddenly placed his own shining bow before him;
for how else could this have happened before such an enraged man, who was like Death personified?
The ritual for saving life is a field of sacrificial offerings extending to the ends of the quarters, even for those who have gone to heaven.
"Even this host of Arimardana, filled with despair, bore the earth in battle"—
having heard this, O most arrogant kings, do not set your pride upon your arms!
Do you not know that his entire conduct is as difficult to perceive as the work of Brahmā?
This very great [river] flows only externally; it does not flow internally. || 98 ||

By the ritual of giving with his hand, he surpassed even the five wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣas*); for as each bud was offered during the performance of the oblation, it became like a finger to him,
and thus he, who had previously possessed only four fingers, became one with five fingers.
Even in the world, this conventional usage would not exist; was it not accepted by those who came before? || 99 ||
He never casts even his sword from his hand against those who act as adversaries;
yet, if he were to touch us—even with a finger—he would consume us along with our allies like dry grass.
For his arrows, which fall upon the surface of the earth in battle, reach even to the far distance.
Alas, alas! What impropriety is this? Even now, the ocean rejoices upon seeing that moon which, though conquered by his own fame, is yet born from his own body;
yet, having encountered the submarine fire with such brilliance, he dries up—oh, how strange!
Every person sees the faults of another, but not their own.

He whose intense luster was like that of a great lordly elephant capable of suppressing the obstruction caused by the multitude of enemy elephants— their pillar-like trunks arrogant with rising pride—

conquered the Lord of Śakra in battle by means of his weapons, and having slain him, he seized four intoxicated elephants as if they were the four expedients (upāyas) personified in the hands of his army, in accordance with his vow of sincere heroism.

Thus ends the first canto, titled "The Description of His Ancestors," in the great epic poem *Śrī Hammīra*, marked by the hero, composed by the great poet Śrī Nayacandrasūri, disciple of the venerable Jayasiṃhasūri. || 9 ||
Now begins the second canto: Then,
due to the absence of his son,
King Siṃha, having established his formidable brother-in-law in his own position and having conquered the six internal enemies, departed for the abode of Hari, which is His very name.
Having attained that kingdom, Bhīmadeva immediately displayed such prowess that no report whatsoever circulated on earth to the effect that there existed any real enemy. (2)
Under the guise of pearls falling from the frontal globes of elephants wounded by the tips of his sword,
he caused the long-accumulated flowers of his fame to fall upon the strength of his enemies' valor.
Even in their dreams, enemies were so afflicted by fear upon seeing him that they abandoned even their beloved sleep;
what use is that sugar which, when being eaten, quickly breaks one's teeth? || 4 ||

Alas, although the examination of virtues and vices is indeed more excellent, nevertheless, let those who are arrogant with pride—even those among the celestial trees—remain so, for he did not show even such courtesy toward supplicants. || 5 ||
Then King Vigraharāja, firmly resolved to subdue the eyes [of his enemies], shone forth;
he who, in the field of battle, shattered the bodies and the pride of his rival monarchs in two ways.
His prowess on earth is like a new sun: it causes the lotus-faces of his enemies to close, increases the ocean of the moonlight of joy, and crushes the Rahu of wicked conduct.
When enraged, he scorched the earth with his own most formidable powers;
thereafter, his mental disposition moistened by compassion, he thoroughly drenched it with the nectar of his fame.
Having slain Śrī Mūlarāja—who was honored by the lotus-feet of the hero Vīravīra, who himself observed fierce and heroic vows—he reduced the Gurjara king to a state of utter exhaustion in battle. (9)
Having conquered the group of six internal enemies and being skilled in statesmanship, the illustrious Gudadeva shone as a god among men;
it is a marvel that the entire world revolves around his fame, just as it does around the lord of poets [the Moon]. 10.

The Creator fashioned this forehead mark for the Lord of Gaurī, whose splendor was intended to be rendered free of obstacles by a mere fragment of his own power; that mark shines even today as the thousand-rayed sun in the form of the sky.
He who imposed no harsh taxes upon his subjects, thinking "I am a deer of the earth," is appropriately so;
yet that he brings joy even to the *cakra* bird (the moon) is a marvel beyond compare for whom? 12.
Even when his majesty blazes forth like the fire at the end of an aeon, the creepers of his enemies' fame do not wither anywhere; this is indeed a source of great wonder.

Terrified on all sides by his majesty, the enemies sought refuge in the waters; for even one who possesses a boat will, in secret, resort to what ought not to be done—alas, the hope for life is indeed endless!
That the heaps of grass in the houses of his enemies were consumed by the flames of his majesty on all sides was only fitting, for the same success was achieved by him even among common people.
Thereafter, there was a beloved of the earth named Vallabharāja, whose splendor was as priceless as the sun,
and who possessed a wealth of form so wonderful that its playful beauty captivated the eyes of Līlāvatī.
Having abandoned their human bodies on the field of battle and hastening toward the realm of the gods,
those rival kings trembled upon seeing him, as if they had suddenly beheld the thousand-rayed sun, their courage and prowess restored by memory alone.
Having observed the boundlessness of his glory— which surpassed even the splendors of the wealth of heaven—
his fame quickly expanded fearlessly throughout the world, as if to rival it and become equally limitless.
From him was born Rāma, the lord of the Bāhuja (Kṣatriya) caste, whose arms were capable of bearing the burden of supporting the entire earth;
by him, having crushed the rising Kharadūṣaṇa, the three worlds were swiftly brought under his control.
May his sword, which unites the glory of victory with the lotus-feet of its Lord while casting away the flesh of enemies,
roar in battle with a radiant splendor from the mass of its blazing majesty.
The sword of this one, with its pure blade, severed the heads of the mountains that were his adversaries;
yet it did not touch blood, for those who are pure do not come into contact with another's [impurity] anywhere.
Then the fierce [king] swiftly seized the mind of King Cāmuṇḍa;
for in his lotus-hand the creeper-like sword shone like the braid of the Goddess of Victory.
His majesty, spread across the earth, surely split even stones;
for if it were not so, how could the fire of gold (Hiraṇyaretas) manifest even today from crystals? 23.

He who, in battle, swiftly struck down the lord of the Śakas— whose consciousness was unimpaired despite his pride— as he fixed his attention on shielding the leaf-patterns upon the jar-like breasts of the wife of Kṛtāntaka.
That king named Durlabharāja, whose fame rivaled the moon, held the earth;
for on the field of battle, by the mere meeting of his brows, he utterly crushed the hosts of his enemies.
Seeing that he had conquered his own self through his fame, I suspect the Three-eyed Lord Śiva was seized by a fit of madness;
for how else could even Maheśvara have developed such a passion for wearing nothing but a loincloth? (26)
It was a marvel that the fire of his majesty, which had been extinguished on all sides by the edges of the swords of enemy hosts,
could not be quenched anywhere by the floods of tears from their wives.
The proud one, having conquered Sahābādīna in battle by the strength of his own arms,
seized his fame— which was as bright as the autumnal moon and earned through countless [deeds]— as his own.
Then there was your son named Duḥśaladeva, whose majesty surpassed the hosts of enemies;
having reached his mind, what various delights did the swan of Dharma not display? (29)
Those very sounds of the war-drums which his enemies made as they fled in terror from him in battles became the sounds of the Vedas for the purpose of taking the hand of the Goddess of Victory.
Having placed Śrīkarṇadeva— who had granted his ears the taste of the nectar of songs sung by the women of the celestial lords—
in battle, he married the sovereign fortune of the kingdom.
When she clung to his hand before the eyes of the world and rolled about upon the necks of rival kings,
did Kālikā not attain the proper dignity of that sword-blade which is as fierce as a venomous serpent?
Therefore, Śrī Viśvala, whose fame was the delight of the entire world, adorned every land;
having uprooted the family of his enemies along with their very foundations, he established sole sovereignty upon the earth.

In whose reign, though it was like an axe for the spreading canopy of the creepers of injustice, it was precisely that very injustice which flourished in the world—whom does this not fill with wonder? (34)

In mountain caves belonging to his enemies' wives, which were pleasure-palaces for the deer-eyed women of his friends, she remained happily with her limbs adorned with ornaments; there, she did not even perceive the rising or setting of the sun.

He who, upon the surface of the earth, instantly drenched with floods of tears from eyes rolling in agitation those enemies who had been slain along with their bodies— enemies whose sins were neutralized by the weight of numbness arising from the touch [of his hand].
Having slain in battle Sahāba— who possessed undiminished majesty and an undaunted army—
the Lord liberated Mālava from the mleccha clans in both ways, thereby manifesting his sovereign power.
Then he adorned the earth with his own brilliant glories; for it was a marvel that when his sword trembled in battle, the crest-jewels of his enemies fell away. (38)
Constantly borne upon the heads of people, swiftly fulfilling their heart's desires, her command became a bringer of auspiciousness, like service rendered to the lotus feet of Śiva. (39)
Having heard of his exquisite charm being sung by throngs of Gandharvas in heaven, which goddess did not desire human birth, so as to attain union with him? (40)
Then there appeared the king known as Ālhaṇadeva, the crest-jewel of those who consider themselves warriors;
at the mere thought of him, even his enemies in the forest trembled like elephants upon seeing a great mountain.
Even when a beggar cried out, "Give!", he who was fond of giving did not say, "No."
There is no such thing as a gift, nor is there even a powerful destiny; it is solely the will of the Lord. || 42 ||
In battles, his sword-blade shone with a luster crimsoned by the blood of severed enemies;
it was as if that very tongue of theirs, which had spoken words of rivalry, had been dragged out by him in combat.

Having drunk in with the cups of our ears that song of such a nature being sung upon the earth, we—who have obtained union with Him through the occasion of a dream—have become possessed of the passionate colors of desire. (44)
Then Bhānala-deva, the crest-jewel of the heads of warriors, wedded the fortune of kingship—he who, having split the array of enemies in battle, made his hand a blower for the path to heaven. (45)
Hearing him being sung of by his own beloved women, Śeṣa reflected:
"There must be someone who supports the earth; having gone there for a moment, I shall behold him. (46)

In battle, his staff-like sword was a playful exercise in the mastery of the merchant’s art, bestowing its own blackness upon the lives of his enemies while seizing their very souls and their fame. (47)

Did the Creator first draw away the splendor of Mount Kailāsa, the abode of Śiva, and the moon—the nectar of nectar—and fashion his fame with it, such that these very objects now appear utterly bereft of beauty in its presence? (48)
Raising her hand in the guise of the Golden Mountain, the Earth spoke thus:
"Neither a donor, nor one possessed of discernment, nor one humble, nor one guided by policy—none other than him was born of me. (49)

Released by her terrified husband halfway along the path, she remained there; yet, as if for the sake of slaying her enemy, she perceived her own new island—though situated within her own country—as being somewhat distant due to the intense brilliance of the cool-rayed moon.

He caused to be excavated a pure lake of excellent water, the very essence of merit, which reached the furthest limits of Puṣkara; it was as if the elephants of the quarters were sporting in its embrace through the guise of the reflections of the surrounding mountains.
Because his glory was so wondrous, that king became renowned as Jñānagadeva;
for having obtained equal gifts from him, who on earth were not wealthy men among the supplicants? (52)

Did the fire of their vital energy, having combined with the smoke of grief and the water of tears from the wives of his enemies, and having immediately become solidified by the winds of their sighs, create these foul days of storm? 53.
It is said that for the sake of practice, the fingers, palms,
and nails of him who desired to perform the rite of universal renunciation were created as the breasts of heaven, the sprouts of the celestial tree, and the jewels of the sky.
While the Creator was enumerating his virtues, he incurred such great exhaustion that even after creating the three worlds, not even a mere fraction of them had been fully realized.

Then, O Bhavadviśvaladeva, the Lord of the Universe, whose abode is the manifestation of the universe, truly nourished the state of being the supporter of all beings within the lotus-stamen of his hand and foot. (56)
The pearls that fell from the temples of the lordly elephants of his enemies, split open in battle,
became the very blossoms upon the spreading creeper of his fame.

Does the Himalaya mountain still shed tears even today because he was defeated by her fame—tears appearing in the guise of the melting rocks of Bhima, which have been softened by the intense heat of his own scorching nature? 58.
Having drunk in his virtues drop by drop, the host of gods, though greatly delighted, remained as if struck dumb with wonder;
alas, they did not take refuge in this king of the gods. (59)
Therefore, the most illustrious Mahendra, whose power is greatest and who is named Jayapāla, shines forth;
for by his flowing tears, the tree of his fame has put forth new sprouts upon the wives of his enemies.

He, whose fame was renowned throughout the universe, did not at all succumb to passion upon seeing the hosts of powerful enemies in battle, nor even upon beholding slender-waisted women in the inner apartments.
The daughters of the lord of serpents, whose splendor surpassed the majesty of the rows of swelling waves in the ocean of milk,
sang of his virtues, charming with the sound of their lutes.
Possessing the qualities of both Bhīṣma and Vasiṣṭha, he was Śrī Gaṅgadeva, a moon to the earth;
by the wind of whose breath the wives of his enemies were tormented, while the seven-flamed fire of his majesty blazed forth.
If the mine of faults, beholding the greatness of his fame and bearing a weight of envy,
has acquired a stain of darkness under the guise of a blemish, he does not release it even today.
Even when facing hosts of enemies numbering more than a hundred, he bestowed upon them the non-trivial splendor of the celestial realm;
yet, even after engaging in fierce battles, his sword was never once deprived of its mother [its scabbard]. 65.
Thinking, "May this person not become a vessel for misfortune while Karṇa and others, who are so exuberant in giving,
are still alive," I believe the compassionate Creator fashioned him as the Indra among the circle of donors.

From him was born Someśvara, the abode of infinite virtues that served as ear-ornaments for the ears of all people in the three worlds; he who sports upon the earth and whose conduct follows the path of imperishable policy. 67.
In battles, the sword-blade, brandished by his own lotus-like hand,
shone as if it were the smoke arising from the fire of anger flickering within, manifesting visibly as it flashed outward.

Which woman did not delight her own heart—which had long been immersed in the flavor of sexual union—by making her lover feel embarrassed after he uttered her name by mistakenly pronouncing her clan? (69)
When the wives of his enemies showered tears upon the fire of his majesty— tears which were, as it were,
oblations of water— the enemy’s desires increased exactly as much as his own, for in the case of a favorable fate, even what is adverse becomes entirely favorable.
How can the king of serpents attain identity with this king?
He supported the earth with a thousand heads, while this one supports it with a single arm alone. (71)
In the great poem *Śrī-Hammīra*, he had a beloved wife named Karpūradevī, who was ever intent on spiritual practice (*rādhana*).
Has not the lotus-born [Brahmā], even now submerged in the waters, performed penance, since his face has been conquered by hers? (79)

"Standing here, that lover might at some point look upon them and become greedy for them"—thinking thus, as it were, they have not granted even the deer-eyed women an opening to enter our hearts. (73)
While she was indeed enjoying the sensual pleasures of the earth with her husband without any hesitation,
she gave birth to a son who was a vessel of honor, just as the quarter of the sky gives birth to the orb of the moon on behalf of Hari.
Bearing a weight of sincere affection, King Pṛthvīrāja celebrated his birth with a grand festival and bestowed upon him the name Jagajjanāhlādakara (the Delighter of the People of the World).
With his slender radiance shattering the web of darkness, that boy, growing day by day, became like the sun—a bringer of auspiciousness to the lotus-eyes of the subjects. (76)
Then, seeing that prince who had reached the further shore of both secular treatises and sacred scriptures,
the Lord bestowed upon him the burden of universal sovereignty and, through yoga, cast off his mortal body.
Having received at the proper time the kingdom bestowed by his father, that lord of the earth shone exceedingly,
like the mountain of sunrise when its light, which destroys the mass of darkness, rises at the break of day.
Though he violently attempted to strike down the qualities [of the senses], he did not succeed in striking them down;
and though he extended harm to the next world, he did not actually inflict such harm upon it.
Though he practiced a dark livelihood, he did not adopt a dark way of life;
by that [purity], he caused no suffering in the next world, nor by that [darkness] did he cause suffering in the next world.

In battle, his sword-blade shone like a lotus with blossoming rows of flowers, under the guise of fresh pearls clinging to its surface from the forceful blows it dealt to the frontal globes of the enemy elephants.
Whose fame as a woman of virtuous vows did not inspire confidence in the minds of even the gentle? Alas, who has not abandoned him, even though he remains steadfast until the end of the aeon?
But for others, even a woman of virtuous vows is no longer virtuous; like a prostitute, she abandons them while they still live.
If it were bound and then awakened, how many moments of consciousness would be useful to one who is living? (89)
In his hair he held Sarasvatī, in his belly the Moon, on his neck Śambhu, and at the tip of his trunk the bull of that [Śambhu];
in the sky he held the celestial elephant trumpeting with rut,
and in his two temples the ill-fame of his enemies wandering through the world, mistaking it for his own glory.
Fie upon the endless nature of enmity, alas, that it throbs even within its own progeny! 83.
The Goddess Lakṣmī, who brought about the state of sleepiness in the lotus-born Brahmā,
herself adorned the deceptive form of that [Viṣṇu] out of passion for Him;
otherwise, how could there have been such a destruction of the weight of the prowess of Bali’s enemy [Rāma]?
In battle, the power of him whose luster was exceedingly radiant became most exultant.
Having lifted up the entire earth, the power of the world’s quarters, mountains, elephants, tortoises, and serpents—
though weary from the burden and desiring to reach the further shore—
beheld that crest-jewel of kings, who is ever resplendent, and under the guise of trembling, they sought refuge in him.
I suspect that they did not abandon her, as if pinned down by the stake of shame. || 85 ||

Having attained supreme humiliation through his own loftiness and burden of fame, Himavat, desiring to once again secure for himself a high position of honor, performed worship of the Lord by offering his daughter and other means; was he not truly deluded, thinking that fame alone could not achieve this for them? || 86 ||

Seated at every crossroads on the banks of the river of the perfected ones— a place covered by the dense shade of wish-fulfilling trees constantly drenched with nectar and overspread with wish-granting gems— the goddesses, while grazing herds of divine cattle as their gift, sang aloud in chorus, their lotus-hands playing with the grace of flutes and lutes to dispel their fatigue.
By that king who constantly caused the surface of the earth to be swept clean,
even the excessive rains sent by fate were made to go beyond the further shore of the ocean; yet,
when those very rains were cast into his own eyes by the women of his enemies, did he not cultivate enmity along with them, for he was one whose beloved had been slain?

If the mass of blood from the streams of marrow flowing from the multitude of heads of kings severed by his sword were to spread, it would have turned the entire surface of the earth into nothing but red;
this description in the *Śrī Hammīra Mahākāvya* is as charming as the Milky Ocean agitated by the rays of the rising, pure moon.
If his fame, as it spreads forth, were not instantly made white [by its own brilliance]. || 89 ||
In that battle where the hero likewise distributed multitudes of excellent arrows, manifesting the power of his pride in an instant,
no one— his mind long bewildered by the fear of having his previously acquired fame severed— resorted either to the practice of charity or to the arrogance of considering himself a warrior.

Thus ends the second canto, titled "The Description of the Ancestors, Beginning with the Illustrious Bhīmadeva," in the great poem *Śrī Hammīra*, marked by the hero, composed by the great poet Śrī Nayacandrasūri, disciple of the illustrious Jayasiṃhasūri.

Now begins the third canto. Then, the western rulers were overwhelmed by Sahābadīna, who, with the speed of his vast power, drove them from the surface of the earth— which was already prone to sleep due to the weight of his own sovereign— leaving them no room to stand.
Having placed before him Śrī Candrarāja—who, by gladdening the mother of all beings, brought his own name to its true meaning, and who had been granted the stage by Gopālacaṇḍa; || 2 ||

Those of noble prowess, having conquered their enemies through the strength of their arms, entered the gateway of the palace of King Pṛthvīrāja, where the ground was made thick with the ichor flowing from the temples of great elephants brought as tribute.
Then,
having been ushered in by the messenger with the words of the Lord, those women, adorned with lovely ornaments,
bowed at the pair of lotus-feet of the lord of the earth and sat down in their respective places. || 4 ||
Beholding them with dejected faces, Pṛthvīrāja spoke to his attendants:
"Do kings not possess prosperity at the end, just as the lotus loses its splendor in the heat of summer?"

Then King Candra spoke to him, who was like the shore of the ocean of milk of eloquent speech shining within his heart, with the luster of his teeth that could scrape the moon’s splendor, spreading forth rays as bright as stars.
O Sahibadīna, whose excellent valor was acquired through the power of asceticism,
you became like a comet portending calamity for the circle of the arms of kings who rule the earth.

"Destroy all the lands of the Nāgaras; O doe-eyed one, burn down their temples! He who, having waged war against the kings of the Bāhuja dynasty, has rendered their lineages overwhelmed by calamity. (8)

O you who possess the splendor of the preeminent ornament of all kings without exception— what kings on earth were there whose mountain caves he did not fill with the throngs of those born of arms (warriors) terrified by his own might?

He who, in battle, led the warrior in an instant to Yama’s abode upon the arena of the field of combat—was he perhaps born again as the son of Bhṛgu? Thus did the clans of heroes, filled with agitation, conjecture. (10)
"Here he has come! Here he has come!"—with these words, their lotus-eyes wide open, they gazed toward all ten directions, yet they remained with unblinking eyes out of fear. (11)
Having uprooted even the crops of rival kings— just as Śambhu formerly did with the three cities—
he established his own preeminent capital at the base of the spear that was the ruin of his enemies' clans.
Overcome by that one who harbors a cruel enmity without cause, these kings have sought refuge in you, O protector; therefore, you alone are the supreme authority. (13)
Having heard these words of hers, which were uttered even while she was restraining her speech yet causing anger,
he drew his beard with the lotus-like hand that rested upon the hilt of his sword.
The lord of men made this vow: "If I do not cast him down at your lotus-feet by binding him with the 'peacock-knot' (mayūrabandha), then I shall never again take pride in my lineage. (95)
Then, while the auspicious moment was occurring under all favorable planetary influences, at a favorable *lagna*, and during the *vijaya* yoga,
Śrī set forth, moving restlessly with a mind agitated by the desire to overcome her adversaries.
Those glances which the women of the city cast toward him as he departed— glances that were not like those of young girls—
became for him, by virtue of their auspicious intent, like the splendor of *dūrvā* grass and parched grain.

For the sake of attaining the complete purity of the great grace that was incessantly bestowed upon them, the excellent hosts of heroes, pure-minded and brandishing the massive sword-staves flashing from their hands, marched forth with great zeal.
The roars of the elephants, lofty and trembling, filled the bellies of heaven and earth;
even the creatures dwelling upon the two mountains were rendered devoid of fortitude.

"When the sun of the enemy's prowess has risen, what indeed can be accomplished by this [my] rising? Thinking thus, as it were, the dust raised by the army of the one whose glory was exerting itself veiled the intensely radiant sun."
In the great poem *Śrī-Hammīra*,

the two rivers formed by the two rows of bamboos became knee-deep due to the clouds of dust raised by the impact of horses' hooves, while the rut-fluid from the army's elephants turned them into streams. (21)
Thus, having warded off his enemies through numerous military expeditions, the king, by means of many departures from this life,
traversed the earth extensively and besieged that kingdom of Śaka kings.
Then, having heard through his spies that he had arrived at the vicinity of his own territory, Śakeśvara—

whose prowess was irresistible— equipped his army, which had brought wretchedness upon its enemies, and took up a position against the foe. Their bodies were adorned with the splendor of the staffs of their bows, and large quivers were fastened to the flanks of their waists.
The Yavana heroes, having minutely observed their enemy warriors with their eyes, departed with their backs turned.
First there were clouds of dust, then the humming of bees circling the temples of the female elephants;
thereafter came the loud lion-roars of the warriors—thus, at that moment, the two armies met.
Beholding one another, their limbs trembled with an intense and spreading agitation;
bearing various flashing weapons, the great heroes advanced to perform the sport of the battlefield.
Where is Indra, whose birth was from the lotus-like hand of the king of the host of warriors, who casts away the fame of swift-retreating trees as if they were mere clusters of jewels? 27.

At that time, the soldiers belonging to Ghaṭaikadeśī fought with great vigor against the horses of Suśobha; as if their latent enmity had been awakened by their mutual glances, they struck out fiercely.
Then, having entered the elephant's trunk, a certain man skilled in the art of striking,
possessed of fierce valor, tore open its belly with a razor-sharp blade and quickly cast it down upon the ground.
Another, leaping with speed from the earth, mounted the high forehead of a lordly elephant;
with his sword-staff playing like a tail, he assumed the grace of a lion.
A certain elephant, seizing a charging horse by its mouth with ease as if it were a crow's beak,
suddenly made it whirl in the air and dashed it against the stony ground of the battlefield.
Having cast [the elephant] behind him with the fierce speed of his trunk under the pretext of causing it to tremble,
the other elephant shone as if personally wielding a sharp-edged spear (paṭṭiśa) to fight, while the foot-soldiers rejoiced.
Hearing the trumpeting of the elephants, a certain horse, becoming terrified,
covered his ears with the fragment of his turban and simultaneously extinguished his desire for battle.
In battle,
he struck with his very tusks— whose tips were piercing— as an elephant charged in fury to kill him.
Another, whose two arms had been severed by his adversary, fought with his teeth alone, engaging in a battle of policy.

What wonder is there for warriors when they pierce through armor, chariots, and well-born bodies, since even their minds were shattered by those [arrows] with such lightness of hand as to be like atoms? (35)

Then, in that calamity, the fathers experienced a flood of joy for their sons in battle such as had not arisen even at the time of their birth for those who were childless— not even a hundredth part of it.
Struck on all sides by fierce and impetuous warriors with the blows of their terrible sword-blows and falling mallets,
the Turuṣkas perished like the families of the one-eyed (Rudras).
Just as was the condition of the *harimantha* beans situated within a mechanical device, such became the state of the Yavana lords who had taken refuge in the battle with King Cāhamāna. (38)
Seeing his own camp shattered in battle like something long decayed, the Lord of the Śakas,
impetuous with rage, himself rushed forward, wielding a sword-staff in his most massive fist.
Beholding him rushing toward me, I too ran forward with intense speed,
my eyes fierce and blood-red with passion, resembling the glowing embers of the fire of anger flickering within.

"Are these two wild elephants that have emerged, difficult to behold with their trunks shining like great sword-blades gleaming from within the hollows of their trunks?"—thus were they conjectured by the ranks of heroes. (49)
Filling the cavities of the worlds with the sounds produced by the striking of their feet,
those two, experts in the practice of mutual blows, waged war for a long time out of fury.
Thus the god among men, fighting in battle,
having forcibly employed some slight stratagem and completely subdued the king of the Śakas, duly fulfilled his vow.
Having brought those lords of the earth who had sought refuge under his own protection through wise policy within his own domain,
that proud king, having reduced the host of his enemies to mere celestial chariots, then returned to his own capital.
Having given him garments of great splendor that inspire longing for the world of the gods, the King released him;
alas, who indeed would wish to engage in such a fierce battle again with one who is filled with the essence of Lakṣmī? || 45 ||
Having thus been defeated seven times by the lord of the earth in various ways on the field of battle,
that cruel Yavana king withered and grew utterly dejected.
In the *Śrī Hammīra Mahākāvya*:

Then, desiring victory over the Lord of Śaka—the one whose banner bears the emblem of Indra’s thunderbolt—by means of his own strength and stratagem, the Lord of Śarpa, longing for power, set forth toward him like the Moon toward the Lord of Planets (Rāhu). (47)

The beautiful splendor of the lords of lands such as Kāmboja, Laṅkā, Hayabhīma, Bhilla, and Vaṅga, and a multitude of horses that were swift, radiant, and beloved for their measured pace, numbering eight hundred thousand well-trained ones. 48.

Then, that king who was like a mere fragment of a jar gave his army— whose martial splendor was agitated by the sudden arrival of the enemy’s defeat— to that king who had spoken of the conduct of self-restraint.
Immediately thereafter, through that spreading grace, this Sahāb-ad-Dīn attained imperial sovereignty.
Having met him, who was unknown to anyone before, he seized Delhi with great prowess.

Then, hearing from the mouths of the people whose splendor was shattered—the people who had repeatedly practiced flight out of fear and who raised a clamor of "Slay! Slay!"—he perceived the arrival of the Lord of the Śacīs.

"Though he has been defeated by me in battle hundreds of times, why does he still act with such restlessness like a child? Thinking thus, the lord of the earth set forth, even though his retinue was meager, as he carried himself with great pride.
Seeing that pair standing before him with their hands raised, trembling from intense fear, Śakra reflected:
"Even alone, he cannot be conquered by us, just as a five-faced lion cannot be defeated by deer. (53)
Then, at night, in the dense darkness, the lord of the Śakas had his trusted agents dispatched;
together with musicians, they bribed his horse-keeper with abundant gifts of gold. (54)
"By good fortune we have met! Surely those of whom we spoke will go to their own supreme abodes.
Today we shall firmly destroy the vast kingdom of our enemies"—thus they spoke to one another with words full of resolve and reasoning. (55)

When only a sliver of the moon remained in the sky and the sun was like a mere glimmer of light, the Śakas, having approached in secret from all sides, descended upon the king’s camp. [56] (A pair of verses:
"Seize the enemy! Subdue him! He is Indra himself advancing swiftly before you!"
"We have struck them down; indeed, they have been slain by these"—thus varied were the words of the fierce warriors.
While the battle was raging on all sides,
that horse named Nāṭārambha, urged by Śakra’s son, neighed loudly and presented itself to the king.
Then, perceiving Pṛthvīrāja mounted upon that horse, those musicians, their hearts filled with apprehension,
played the mṛdaṅga, bherī, paṭaha, and other instruments— sounds dear to the most excellent of heroes. (59)
Hearing the sound of the musical instruments— which surpassed the deep trumpeting of elephants with their uplifted trunks—
the king was momentarily embarrassed as the Garuda, like a peacock, began to dance.
"Take courage! Do not despair!"—with these words the Yavanas quickly approached;
what was to be done? Like sparrows, they suddenly surrounded this foolish man and bit him.
Touching the earth with his right foot and his big toe, while his left foot was drawn up and bent,
and carrying a sword and a shield in his hand, he then leaped up and sat upon the ground.
Terrifying some with the knitting of his eyebrows, others with the rolling of his fierce eyes, and still others with lion-like roars,
that Indra among the circle of warriors waged a battle of wondrous variety for a long time.

Then a certain Śaka, approaching from behind, threw a bow around the king's neck and drew it taut; he quickly struck the monarch down, and afterwards, all of them joining together, bound him with force. (64)
Then he, the beloved of the earth, who was tranquilized by a multitude of excellent virtues, who had repelled the host of the wicked, and who was radiant with mature majesty—
Through the play of destiny, having obtained a husband from Śakra,
the lord of the gods, she experienced pleasure twice over— both in eating and in living.
Then, seeing that the soldier Purodayarāja had arrived— sent by the Lord himself from the territory of the Yavana king— he entered the city from the Śaka region, having cast aside all fear.
Hearing of the king's misfortune, Udayarāja cried out, "Alas! It has happened;
it could not have been otherwise," and he shook his head repeatedly and violently, as if to extract that thorn from his own heart.
"If I were to abandon this master who has fallen into calamity and depart, then shame would seize my play; thus, may there be happiness for the Gauḍa lineage.
Having reflected thus, he completely besieged the city of Indra from all sides.
He remained there for two fortnights, fighting with persistence day after day.
Once, a certain person, with a sorrowful mind, spoke thus to this king of the Mlecchas:
"Who was it that released you from him many times in battle? Alas! You have abandoned him not even once."

Hearing those words of his, which were consistent with righteousness, that cruel-minded man became exceedingly enraged. He spoke thus: "Let these people be told: 'Flee from this very place! This is the secret doctrine for provoking the anger of the King.'"

Then, while the lords of heroes cast their gaze upon the surface of the earth, and while the crowds of the virtuous— whose sprouts of grief were instantly watered by the flow of copious tears from shame— stood there,
he, burning with fierce rage, brought that king to the edge of a precipice; alas, the base wretches on all sides became blind and deaf to the deliberation of what ought and ought not to be done.
That which the Śaivas call "Śiva," which the Buddhists declare as the "Sugata," and which those devoted to the Arhat doctrine cite as the "Omniscient One"—
that wondrous Brahman, consisting of consciousness, he remained there with a steady mind, remembering it.
King Pṛthvīrāja, the ornament of the circle of kings, attained eternal auspiciousness. || 72 ||
Having heard this news of the king’s destruction,
that young sun to the lotus-stalk of the Gauḍa dynasty was deeply distressed; he returned to his own place along with his army.
Having fought, he attained the station of the Lord of Heaven by means of his prowess. || 73 ||
Having thus learned of the king’s misfortune, King Harirāja, his eyes filled with flowing tears,
performed the funeral rites and subsequently took possession of the entire earth in his own hands.
His fame, which has been heard to be like a flood of nectar poured out in every name and form,
is thick with the spreading dust of camphor;
yet his virtues did not become mere travelers upon the path of words, for that path is muddied by the appearance of the mire of [mere] descriptions.
Is it not a marvel that even those various poets possess qualities such as grandeur and the rest? 75.
Because Lakṣmī indeed took hold of his hand as a lotus, and because he followed her out of passion without guile, Hari himself became the son of those two, Pratāpa;
he, having heard that the enemy of his elder brother was the foe of Smara (Śiva), burned him with anger.
Just as he was unable to distance himself from the Gaṅgā for even a single moment, so it remained with him. || 76 ||

With rays rising from the lofty peaks of his own fame upon the wheel of the earth—rays which, having struck the cosmic egg with a terrifying force, subsequently returned—he made the heavens beautiful with the ever-shimmering waters of the celestial Gaṅgā and possessed of a burgeoning splendor;
for what purpose did he perform this description of Pṛthvīrāja’s battle, so that even the gods might offer it to the pot-born sage Agastya? (77)
The moon has lost its splendor; the Gaṅgā is without waves; the golden mountain (Meru) is no longer bright; Śiva has abandoned his pride;
the elephant of Indra is devoid of rut; and the ocean is not surging with its waves.
The conch resounds in every direction within the flood of his fame.
Whichever kings those prostrating [princes] passed by, they became instantly visible; whichever kings they bypassed and served on all sides, they withered in an instant.
For that lord of the earth, the abode of majesty, during the festival of his world-conquering expedition, there was no other wandering lamp that shone more intensely than his army.

For him who was intent on conquering the quarters and traversing the entire surface of the earth, the ocean became an obstacle to his horses as they ran with exceeding speed, causing their gait to falter—
just as the assembly of those who are clever in debate becomes an obstacle to the words of a poet whose brilliance shines through the investigation of the subject matter.
Having slain the lords of the earth who were his adversaries, he caused them to obtain all their own wealth;
and perceiving in their hearts this very act of his as a service rendered to them, they too, in an instant,
honored him with gifts of elephants, horses, kings, land, treasuries, and so forth.
Vain is the merit produced by helping others who are worthless, even if it is done toward an enemy. (89)
Having offered the oblation of his enemies as a sacrifice into the mouth of the fire of his own wrath,
he caused such a torrential rain to fall incessantly upon this earth that it was nourished by the abundant tears falling from the eyes of the wives of those slain heroes.
Just as the sprout of the seed of injustice quickly took root so as not to perish, [82]
