As he wandered along, the bride-like rows of forest trees seemed to beckon their own beloved, the Lord of the Earth, for an embrace with their lotus-hands of trembling shoots, shaken by the breezes from Mount Malaya.
In every forest, the bees, their flight slackened by drinking honey,
appeared upon the trees like pellets from the flower-bow of the Lord of Arrows as he practiced his aim with a string of pellets.
Even by its mere sight, and by the power of separation from it, causing the trembling of the body,
the Palāśa tree with its crest-like top quickly attained in this world the fulfillment of its own name.
As soon as my foot touched it, this Aśoka tree— already thirsting for contact with me—
seemed to grow angry that I was now a woman whose husband had gone away, and it made me tremble again and again with its violent blossoming.
Enticing swarms of bees with its sweet nectar through its union with honey, the Tilaka tree attained a preeminent beauty among all trees, like a mark of distinction.
Even without the sprinkling of the nectar from her mouth, the Bakula tree, bearing a splendor beyond the reach of words, surpassed all the mental composure of beautiful-eyed women. 24.
In the rows of forest trees that had blossomed at their own appointed time during the nights of the unseasonable season,
the buds of the *campaka* tree attained the likeness of the lamp-flames of King Smara.
In the lake, where the clusters of bees were deeply settled upon the petals of exceedingly blue lotuses,
the splendor of the newly risen moon shone forth in the sky through the lotuses that had blossomed with shimmering beauty.

Resembling a cluster of blooming palāśa flowers, the young man appeared like one performing the penance of fire-sacrifice with his head, bearing the grief of separation from Mālatī as if it were a mass of soiled water-drops.
The forest creepers shone exceedingly with the Malaya and other winds that had caressed them,
as if they were performing long-cherished embraces with one another after a period of separation.

In the fragrant breeze, she shone as she fanned the Lord of Ananga— who was joined by drops of perspiration and possessed the power to conquer the entire three worlds— with plantain leaves trembling in the wind.
"Worship the Lord of your heart; abandon this pride immediately, for the time has indeed passed"—as if awakening the fawn-eyed women with these words, the young cuckoo warbled beautifully.
"Is this a kiss, or is it sweet honey?"— as if making such a distinction,
the bee, devoted to sweetness, kissed the lotus for a moment and then the face of the female bee for a moment.
In this spring season, O playful lady, some bees here seem to say to the ignorant,
"This is this, that is that," with their humming sounds as they hover over various flowers.
Exceedingly calming the youthful minds of his companions as they were intent on coaxing their beloveds,
the sweet-voiced cuckoo, intoxicating his mate with his melodious warbling, repeatedly embraced and kissed her.
With blossoming clusters of flowers as their beautiful breasts and new sprouts for their wonderful hands and feet,
the creepers shone like forest deities who had arrived in the spring to behold him.
In the act of applying unguents to their bodies, the women increasingly favored the flame-tipped incense;
for how can a thing that has long been a source of benefit suddenly be discarded here? 35.
As if weighed down by the heavy sins born of having terrified the wives of travelers,
the bees— possessing the dense luster of collyrium and fuel for the sacrificial fire— shone as they wandered through every forest.

Having thus observed this season of spring, which forcibly strikes down all joy with its pair of glances, and having questioned that hero who is the beloved of the victorious world, the excellent elder brother of the prince [spoke]. (37)
By the grace of those women who had ascended their faces with the desire to behold his matchless beauty,
he created the expanse of the sky, even during the day, as if it were filled with many shimmering lunar discs.

He was sweet with the beautiful women of the harem who desired to engage in forest sports, having prepared divine fragrances from heaps of camphor, the finest musk, sandalwood, and the pollen of nāgaja flowers.

He, whose moon-like face was radiant with youthful laughter and jesting, proceeded toward the city grove, which was graced by rows of trees shimmering with breezes that played among swaying clusters of leaves.
Then,

adorned with ever-new and shining ornaments, young men wearing fine garments sang to the naked Arhat; they were intoxicated by the festival of spring, and their bodies shone with a radiant luster that was sweet and intoxicating.
O friend, even though your lotus-face was adorned with festive ornaments, it now weeps out of a desire to weep for you;
come quickly and, having thoroughly propitiated this beloved, destroy the joy of your enemies. (42)
Thus, having reflected deeply for a long time in her heart upon the words of a certain dear friend,

she cast aside her pride, approached her husband, and displayed a charm of clear affection. (43) [Yugmam] While another woman, moon-faced, was skillfully employing various gestures to conciliate him, he—
She was embraced by him at that very moment, she who had previously signaled her intention through her gestures.

"O rogue, what is he doing to you with his face bent down by a tremor of agitation due to separation from you?"—saying this, a certain woman brought her toward her beloved under a pretext and handed her over to him. 45.
The braid of hair of a certain lotus-eyed woman, fallen at her feet to win her favor,
shone like the sword of the flower-armed god [Kāma] intended to cut through her pride.
Alas! Look, O lady with a face like a flower; how do these sweet days of spring pass away so suddenly?
Even now, maintaining this pride, what indeed do you intend to achieve that is harmful to yourself and others? Alas! 47.
Thus, a certain virtuous man, skilled in conciliation, having appeased his enraged beloved with words of entreaty,
performed the act of a honey-bee by offering her embrace at every step.
"You do not look at him, nor do you give him a word; how then shall this follower of yours live?
Hearing these words of her beloved, the other woman, already intoxicated from drinking wine, attained an even greater state of intoxication.
Then, beholding the forest— which had hands of waving fresh shoots, which possessed a mass of bees for its braided hair, and which bore beautiful clusters of flowers for its breasts—
they felt a longing to sport there, as if looking upon a newly wedded bride.
When the host of young women was intent on performing a cruel act upon her,
the trees seemed to tremble under the guise of swarms of bees fluttering on their leaves, stirred by the blowing wind.

Having abandoned the beautiful blossoms of the forest all around, a certain lotus-faced woman was intensely agitated by swarms of bees seeking warmth, which fell upon her face with the mistaken notion that it was a lotus.
Where was she not embraced by him as he lifted his beloved onto the tip of a creeper?
And where was a nail-scratch not inflicted upon her body—that which, being fixed there, produced how much joy in her heart? (53)

Suddenly displaying her two well-rounded breasts, which she had clasped in her own hands, the beautiful-eyed woman laughed— even though she was angry— saying, "Tell me, by whom indeed have your breasts not been measured as being exactly this size?"
O beloved, saying "This flower has a sweet fragrance," Vidura, intent on his purpose, brought it near under the pretext of offering it to the lion and placed his hand upon her lip. 55.
"If you grant me a single kiss upon the face, then I shall give you this flower garland"—
when her husband spoke thus, another woman, understood by her friend, replied with both bashfulness and joy.
As her beloved climbed the tree, another woman quickly seized his foot, mistaking it for a leaf;
she neither pulled it away nor let it go, as the thrill of attaining him caused a spreading horripilation to arise within her.
"O moon-faced one, behold, most delightful blossoms are shimmering upon the creepers ahead!"—
thus deceiving his beloved, the other led her to a secluded spot for the sake of pleasure.
"O, where has this cluster of flowers gone even while I was looking?"—uttering such deceptive words, a certain man, laughing, took the beloved’s breast from her hand and said, "It has been found. 59.
"O, where has this cluster of flowers gone from my sight?"— uttering such deceitful words and intent on searching everywhere,
he crushed the pair of breasts belonging to many young women.
A swarm of bees, greedy for the nectar dripping from fresh blossoms bound upon her slender creeper-like arms, was embraced by that most clever woman under the guise of a tree. 61.

With her consciousness stolen away by the sight of the lord of her heart who had ascended to the state of being her fruit, she addressed the other woman in vain, saying, "Give me back my husband! Give me back my husband! (52)

Sent by the other [the sun] with a multitude of flowers from the grove of the mountain-splitter (Indra), he was struck down by your sighs; disregarding her, why did he rise toward that [other woman]? 63.

"O, look, look! How the young bee flits about the *lakuca* and *sukucu* fruits before us!"—having thus enticed his beloved, the other gazed at her for a long time with a sidelong glance and drank her in deeply. 64.

The bees, making loud humming sounds as their chief characteristic, obstructed [the path] to the utmost degree like forest guards, having placed themselves with effort upon their heads due to the abundance of blossoming flowers on the rows of trees.
Holding between them a curtain as it were— a veil for the purpose of warding off the heat—
the gambler, having enticed the woman who was the sovereign of his heart, kissed her fearlessly.
Fanning her with handheld fans of blooming *bhāsika* flowers woven by his own hands,
that other man, skilled in the arts of love, deeply won over the fair-eyed woman even though he had previously acted against her wishes.

As she seized the flowers situated on the tips of the trees with her upward-reaching hands, another woman shone for a moment like an immense power becoming manifest from a very slender belly, as her garment slipped down.
When the rogue held her lower lip under the pretext of a sprout,
the smile that his beloved displayed became indeed the very fame of his manifest skill in deceit, shining like the moon.
Holding his beloved— who had turned her body away with her limbs grown rigid— by one arm,
while grasping a lotus with his other hand, that supreme being shone like the God of Love bearing his bow and arrow.
As a woman climbs the trunk of a tree to gather flowers,
her right foot remains on the ground while her left touches a branch; then,
having employed some artifice, another man bends down until his head reaches the region below her navel.
Seeing this, his desire was aroused, and he conceived no small longing for sexual union with her.
"If you give me this flower standing at the tip of the branch, then, my dear, I shall certainly grant whatever you ask"— when this was said by another charming woman,
she quickly led her friend away, took the flower, and gave it [to her] under a pretext.
That which had been in the hearts of both of them was brought forth by the rogue.
With the long branches of their lotus-like hands grasped by one another, and their lotus-feet joined together,
those lotus-eyed women, being gently swayed by their female companions, themselves attained the likeness of a swing.
On the surface of the earth, where the forest of sprouts had been scattered and torn away by the tips of the nails of amorous women,
the rows of flowers shone like strings of pearls upon a vast vessel of coral.
With their bodies adorned by rows of fresh garments, bracelets, and clusters of flower-ornaments, the beautiful-eyed women shone like soldiers clad in armor for the king whose weapon is flowers.
Thus, by means of these most auspicious and charming modes— consisting of series of expansive sports manifested through the enjoyment of contact with their own limbs—
the women of the city instantly brought the floral splendor of the forest, arising at the time of the Lord of Seasons, to its state of fruition.

Thus ends the fifth canto, titled "The Description of Spring," in the great poem *Śrī Hammīra*, marked by heroism, composed by the great poet Śrī Nayacandrasūri, disciple of the venerable Śrī Jayasiṃhasūri.

Now begins the sixth canto: Then, seeing the young men perspiring from the influence of their sporting in the forest, the prince went toward the lake of Jaitrasāgara, which possessed the beauty of a fresh pool, in order to engage in water-sports.
The rows of trees on its banks shone with a luster like the fluttering wings of white cranes, appearing like the army of Siṃhikā’s son spreading out all around the lunar orb. || 2 ||

With the beauty of its city named Stambhana, which was more delightful than any other and preceded by battles reflected within its waters, it truly laughed at the Lord of the Heart of Rivers (the Ocean), whose gateway is the vast mouth of the Kāverī. || 3 ||
That [lake], with its green emerald and pearl-like clusters smiling through the blue palāśa leaves of trees growing on its banks,
bore the likeness of an elegant ear-ornament for the Earth, the lady of the world.
Bearing a fullness of nectar manifested under the guise of rows of petals from blue lotuses,
he shone upon having descended to earth like the lunar orb appearing out of fear of Rāhu.

Under the guise of lotuses blossoming with rising pupils—the bees wandering upon their pericarps—it seemed as if they were gazing at their own fortune; thus, he possessed hundreds of eyes. (6) Then, with their long hips and moving glances, the women blocked the forest path with a tinkling sound. (A *kulaka* of six verses.)
As if wishing to restrain their lords of life who were desirous of going forward to offer salutations, they [stood] before them.
Beholding their own splendor reflected in the water, young women quickly drew away their minds from their mirrors;
for what indeed can hold the hearts of women, once they have found that upon which they may dwell for a long time?
In the waters of the great lake Uttaraṅgiṇī at the glorious Hammīra-mahākāṭha,
women gathered blossoming flowers as if they were offering them to the Lord of the Mountain (Śiva) in his watery form, desiring to revive him from his love for Pārvatī.
As the faces of the graceful women standing on the bank were reflected in the water, swarms of bees, thinking them to be blooming lotuses, alighted upon them and made the throngs of youths laugh.
Because they were designated as the radiant reflections of those young women who frequented the waters, the goddesses of the lotuses appeared as if to offer them hospitality. 11.

Then, having somehow seized with their hands the slender-waisted women whose bodies were trembling with fear upon seeing the bottomless waters, the young men laid them down upon the surface of the water. 12.
"O charming girl, do you not see even your own friend who is performing water-sports right before you? Saying this and showing her his own reflection, another clever man, alas, consoled her.
"There is deep water here; therefore, O charming girl, it is not proper for you to enter," having said this, the gambler placed the fawn-eyed woman upon his chest and plunged in.

Though intensely eager for water-sports and held back by her lover at the edge of the bank, a certain woman remained exactly as she was, her soul surrendered to the sentiment of the joy of beholding him; and so too did the other.
Though devoid of consciousness, that pond, when struck by the slopes of the breasts of young women, suddenly entered a state of agitation; the cause of this was its very essence of rasa.

The water first touched the hips of the young women, which were restless from contact with their bodies; thereafter it played upon their breasts. Alas, where does the sense of order manifest in the dull-witted? 17.
The water of that lake, though knee-deep, became exceedingly neck-deep, as if it had attained great abundance through the salt washed down from the limbs of women.

Even the bees abandoned the lotuses that had bestowed their honey since birth and took refuge in the faces of the deer-eyed women; for how can there be discrimination toward those who are stained? (19)

With her lotus-face and darting eyes casting glances that resembled the lunar disc, she was seized by the ruddy geese (*cakravāka*) as they approached to devour the lotus-fibers; yet she was neither released nor consumed by them.

The waters, flowing down the mountain paths during their childhood, were repeatedly splashed against the rugged slopes of the banks; now, as they flowed over the high breasts of women, those same waters were again obstructed by them.
While your beloved was taking water in his cupped hands to sprinkle upon the face of his dearest one during their water-sport,
he released it only after seeing your reflection therein, fearing that it would break the surface.
The beloved one was sprinkled by the intoxicating-eyed woman with the power of her noble lineage during the libation;
he was seized by her arm upon her slight throat, as if by a hand skilled in the art of arrow-duels.

When her lover drank from the lotus-face of the intoxicated woman— the face which was like a blossoming lotus— the bees, under the guise of her falling drops of water and her mass of hair, seemed to weep with tears of sorrow.
Through the streams of water released by those women from the gaps between their tightly pressed rows of teeth,
the god of love became one whose weapon was water, for the purpose of quenching the fire-weapon of their husbands' pride.
When she stood in water reaching up to her neck, the Lord of Life (the Moon), moving with the gait of an elephant,
perceived her lotus-face situated between the two lotuses [of her feet] by the loss of its luster.
"Shrī has been carried away from our eyes by these bees"— thus harboring anger,
the fair-eyed women repeatedly submerge and then raise up lotuses in the lakes.
In the water, by way of metaphorical designation, Madana and Rati were, as it were, invertedly transferred—
Madana taking on the specific excellence of the bridegroom’s beauty, and Rati that of the bride’s— each having resorted to the other.
Having gained access to one woman through deceitful hand-movements, a certain man,
whose passion was known and manifested, repeatedly kissed another who was turned away from him, like a bee toward a lotus.

Upon the breast-slopes of the women, as hard as the core of a mountain, where the pearl necklaces had slipped like rows of foam from falling waters, the strings of pearls shone like a line of foam upon a lake. (30)
On the bodies of the women, the nail-marks made by their lovers shone as the unguents were washed away by the water, appearing like mantra-syllables intended for the eradication of rival wives.
Even when emerging from the water, the pearl-oysters did not release their necklaces because their holes were filled with water;
for who, having attained the pleasure of touching the pair of breasts of beautiful-eyed women, would ever abandon it? (32)
On her tremulous lotus-foot, the anklet, rendered silent by the force of the flood of water,
resounded clearly within the secret chamber of the deer-eyed woman, like a *guhyaka* in a banyan tree that remains unperceived.
Wandering in water reaching up to her neck, the woman assumed the guise of a lotus with its petals clearly displayed;
thus did her friend’s mind, trusting upon beholding her face, quickly conclude that it was a blooming lotus.
In the great battle of Śrī Hammīra, when the Lord [the enemy] approached the Bhāvanā dancers and touched their thighs with his hand while he was within the water,
the slender-waisted women— whose bodies were trembling from the javelins— were gazed upon by their friends with eyes struck by wonder. (35)
With droplets of water from her tears made rough by the rays of her lover’s teeth, the intoxicating-eyed woman,
her limbs bristling with horripilation born of joy, shone as if pierced by the shafts of the God of Love.
Even though its fragrance had been released by her sporting in the water, the moon-faced lady did not cast away her flower garland;
for one who possesses virtue is not easily abandoned even by oneself, how much less so when he is the very essence of one's life? (37)
When the lotus-eyed woman’s waist-cloth was playfully snatched away by her lover, the lotus plant—certainly assuming the role of a friend—offered her its own petals as if they were garments. (38)
The blackness that had been washed away from the face of the young woman by her husband with his unconquered eyes,
quickly returned to a state of manifestation upon entering the lotus-like face of another impatient woman.
Thinking the lotus raised for the purpose of striking her to be the face of his beloved, he kissed it;
oh, what another rogue was there who made her laugh even as she turned her face away with a smile! 40.
The anklets of the women sporting in the water did not produce their tinkling sound;
for what person devoted to virtuous conduct would expand his own greatness in the midst of water? (41)

In the lake water, even as the lotus-faced women were being pulled about by one another out of mutual excitement, the Goddess of Fortune was attained in her highest form by the clusters of flowers; for where would blossoms not find a place within the presence of beauty?
The couple, their faces beautiful with rice, lotus stalks, and grain held in their hands, drank of love as it were, their eyes half-closed under the influence of gazing at one another. (43)

In the forest of her smiling lotuses, how could anyone else have known the lotus-face of the lotus-eyed one, had she not herself, out of guile, watered the [other] lotuses? For she alone was utterly bewildered. 44.
Though struck on the petal of her lower lip by him— who, mistaking it for a blooming lotus, had kissed it—
another woman did not realize that she was truly bitten by her lover’s face, even though it was the plain truth.
The fresh red dye of lac was washed away from the lips of the tremulous-eyed women by the waters;
yet it produced an even greater adornment there, through the tooth-marks left by their lovers.
The ornament of women with restless eyes is water that removes the stain of collyrium with a mere drop;
yet tell me, does even a destroyer of dull-witted intellect ever attain proficiency in performing a task? (47)
Description of Water-Sports:
A certain fish-eyed woman, seeing her own lotus-face reflected in the water, mistook it for a fish within a lotus bud;
as she reached out to seize it, she instead captured the heart of her beloved. (48)
When the waters were thick with the heavy kohl from the eyes of women laughing, the young men thought: "Is this not the blessed daughter of the Sun (Yamunā), mingled with the waters of the Gaṅgā? 49.
"Come quickly; O fair-limbed one, I shall show you your friend hidden among the lotuses"—deceiving his beloved with these words, a certain man won her over in a secret wager. (50)
In the lake-like waters of the Sarayū, where the lotuses were submerged as the river rose due to the weight of the mature clouds,
the faces of the women became like lotuses through the swarms of bees gathering under the guise of their tresses.
As the lotus-eyed women stood on all sides in the shallow water, their breasts shone forth clearly and heaved with great force due to the ease of their swimming;
they appeared like wheels whose spokes have met at the hub, with their own lovers standing close by.
During the mutual splashing of water, a woman, her neck bent and agitated by the excessive drenching,
beheld her own braid reflected in the water resting upon her back;
fearing it was her lover, she embraced it with great trepidation.
Thinking that he might seize it with his own sword-blade, he threw his hand at her once more.

The flood of water quickly loosened the mass of their tresses, kissed even their lotus-eyes, rolled upon the surface of their breasts, reached the slopes of their hips, and touched their feet—just as a lover does to his beloveds. ||54||
The knot of her braided hair has loosened, all the collyrium from her eyes has washed away,
and the red dye of her lips has faded; her entire body is covered with incessant horripilation,
and even the decorative leaf-patterns painted upon her cheeks and breasts have vanished as her strength is lost.
The water-sports of the young women became, as it were, the very gateway for the entry of the essence of passion. ||55||
The mass of waves, stirred by the radiance of their hips, breasts, and rows of teeth, which were tremulous with the act of emission,
suddenly flashed like water splashing against the riverbank as if it were accompanying them on their journey.
Then, with their wings parted by hearing the loud sound produced by the falling of their feet due to extreme eagerness,
the couples emerged from the water sportively, finding their mark by striking one another’s palms.
In the *Śrī-Hammīra-Mahākāvya*, observe how the garments of the women, drenched by the water, did not cling to them due to their translucency;
surely, out of fear of being cast off, they remained hidden within the luster of their bodies. (58)
Even when their gait was colored by passion, the bodily splendor of those slender-waisted women did not diminish;
for the natural beauty of a person, any ornament serves merely as an auspicious addition. (59)
The long, pure tresses of hair hanging down on the backs of the women who had emerged from the lake appeared,
as it were, like touchstones placed upon golden bands to test their purity.
The long, trailing mass of hair on the backs of the young women who had emerged from the lake shone like the plumage of a peacock perched upon a rock of Mount Meru.
The bodies of the womenfolk, being excessively adorned with the soft hems of their garments,
appeared like the sharpened weapons of the flower-arrowed god (Kāma), who had set his mind upon conquering the entire three worlds.

With their opening blue-lotus eyes, waves of lovely beauty rippling from the play of their creeper-like brows, and charming with the moss of their loosened tresses, those women appeared like female cranes upon a lake. (63)
"Because he has seized our enemy's ornaments, this man carries water [for his ablutions]";
thinking thus, as if out of great indignation, the women bound him with their masses of hair, which resembled swirling whirlpools.
Having thus performed this water-sport, which was not produced by any other [king],
that heroic Hamīra, the son of Śrījaitrasaṃha,
dismissed these people, each to their respective homes.
Having bestowed his favor upon the supplicant, he entered his own residence.

Thus ends the sixth canto, titled "The Description of the Water-Sports," in the great poem *Śrī Hammīra*, composed by the great poet Śrī Nayacandrasūri, disciple of the venerable Śrī Jayasiṃhasūri, which bears the mark of a hero.
Now begins the seventh canto:
Then the sun, with its rays, adorned the crest of the western mountain as if proclaiming with its beams the minds of the tremulous-eyed women who were longing for the arrival of the end of night. (1)
No one indeed was able to disregard her who had fallen into calamity by the power of fate;
for it is as if the orb of the sun, appearing to be afflicted by disease, becomes an orb from which its radiance has vanished. ||2||
"Is it because they clearly call me 'the winged one' (pataṅga) in this world that these [rays] have placed me among the moths?"—
bearing as it were such indignation toward the wise, the sun took birth with a crimson body. (3)
With his body overcome by the great fatigue of moving incessantly through the sky, the sun entered the middle of the river like one desiring to play in the water. 4.
May the moon-disk, which causes the daughter of the ocean (Lakṣmī) to mistake the single breast on her lotus-like hand for the chest of the Lord reclining upon the waters,
and which is submerged in the waters of the ocean, bestow prosperity upon the worlds.
When the sun, the eye of the world, has set, darkness settles upon the dull-witted;
it was indeed only natural that you too then brought the entire world under your own power.
When the sun, the beloved of the lotus-lake, had departed somewhere beyond the path of vision,
the splendor of the day entered with affection the fire of the passion belonging to the western quarter.
When the sun, the beloved of one particular lake, departed for another state of woe with its light fading away,
the darkness of grief entered the hearts of the lotuses as if under the guise of the swarm of departing bees.

Beholding her husband, the lord of lights, fallen here into such calamity by the decree of fate, the lotuses immediately closed their petals; for this [closing] was abandoned by their friends, the rays of light.
"Even this white-rayed moon, though possessing the deer-mark, has a dark heart; so too is the bride of the Night.
Therefore, what is there left to behold here?"—thus thinking, the lotus-plant closed her eyes, which were like lotuses.
At the close of day, as if desiring to conquer the bird [the sun] that was shimmering from drinking the light of the moon,
the hosts of those separated from their lovers fell at night and drank the entire heat of the sun.
Did these [lotuses] spread their heat even further than the sun’s rays out of fear of non-attainment?
For now, O Chariot-footed One (Cakravāka), the pairs of birds are unable to endure being together. (12)

At night, as he fell while separated from his mate, the lotus stalk remained caught in the motionless beak of the crane; it shone like a bolt placed there to obstruct him as he sought to depart, unable to endure the grief of separation from his beloved.
Even the serpent-king, though possessing many coils, could with difficulty bend his body between those two as they moved together;
nor did even the lover of the rivers (the ocean) come within the range of memory regarding the simultaneous display of those two who had taken their positions.

The beloved of Rati and Jīvita, who holds the entire world under his own sway, as if issued a command to those who beheld him with longing, under the guise of the sound from the rows of drums resounding at the close of day. 15.
In the great poem *Śrī-Hammīra*, it is said that even the mass of darkness and the power of the sun once occupied lowly positions under his sway;
for this was the first quality of one desiring conquest: the endeavor to bring even those equal to oneself under one's control. (16)
Like sparks from the blazing fire of grief of women whose cruel lovers had been struck by the arrows of Love,
the fireflies shone most intensely at every step, creating a spectacle for the eyes.
Out of extreme cleverness, the unchaste woman did not come within the range of his sight while feigning confusion;
she was delighted by the employment of various stratagems, as if she had been granted a boon by the God of Love himself. (18)
"Why does this darkness fall upon me again and again every day, even though I cast it away so forcefully?
As if in anger at this thought, the moon rose with a body as red as fire. 19.
It was indeed to pacify the darkness that the moon, the bringer of nectar, rose slowly and gradually;
yet that very deer-mark on his lap has become greedy for the grass offered by Indra’s beloved wife.

By the friction of the arrows of Love, which were nourished by the blood arising from the piercing of the various worlds, the orb of the moon was as if reddened; thus it bestowed beauty upon both the sky and its own self.
Under the guise of a mass of thick, spreading hair as white as the teeth of a saw,
the moonlight issued forth from his mouth like a heap of Himalayan sandalwood dust for the sake of his nocturnal beloved.
Holding him— who was situated in the center of her heart— aloft under the guise of his most manifest mark, the moon,
out of excessive affection, surpassed Paśupati, who bears his beloved on half his body, by means of the night.
Having abandoned the lotuses, she who is marked by the glances of the beloved of Hari [is seen]. 24.
To meet her beloved, the moon, the Night assumed a marvelous ornament that surpassed even the dawn:
a lattice-work of fresh pearls consisting of the guise of clusters of stars rising incessantly.
Upon meeting after a long separation, the Goddesses of Fortune embrace the Lord of the Twice-born;
their pearl necklaces break, and the sky becomes starry with the various pearls scattering upward.
Having cast aside his excellent arrows, he whose weapons were fine regarded the moonbeams as being in their stead;
for those who desire ever-new things, even a familiar object becomes a great enemy.
