Having bestowed the kingdom upon King Hammīra, Viṣṇu said to me as I lay sleeping at the end of the night: "Be devoted to the service of wine; what shall I do for you, O Noble One? (54)
Then, having rendered him powerless by force, the playful lord of the earth seized the fortune of sovereignty from Hammīradeva, who was of noble mind and unwilling.
Then, in the great poem of Śrī Hammīra, while serving [the king] in the year nine-fire-and-fire (1399), in the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha,
on the lunar day of Pauṣī, on a Sunday, under the Puṣya asterism, at the tip of the sword when its strength was indicated by the astrologers— (56)

First the family priest, then the moon of the earth (the king), then other lords of the land, then the ministers, then the great merchants, and finally the subjects performed his consecration. (57) [A pair of verses.]
When the umbrella, white as the moon, was held over him by those who provided shade, it was truly extraordinary that its shadow encompassed the entirety of the three worlds. (58)
Then, as if to announce to the world that they would thus repeatedly fall at the feet of that protector of the earth,
the two chowries shone as they descended upon the head of the king.
At that time, the bards recited [panegyrics], auspicious musical instruments were about to sound,
those skilled in dance began to dance, and circles of singers sang songs.
At every step, garlands of salutations appeared radiant, like playful creeper-like eyebrows upon the rows of houses whose doors served as eyes. 61.
Scattered on both sides along the royal roads, heaps of blossoming flowers shone like the wide-spread smiles of the Goddess of the Earth directed toward her beloved and new bridegroom.
Simultaneously with the height of their joy, the lands of Udra, sprinkled with fresh water from Bāhlīka,
shone as if they had manifested their own passion upon a new heart.

I suspect that even the city itself became impassioned upon obtaining the new sovereign, Hamīradeva, under the pretext of the crimson and saffron-colored banners raised high above the peaceful water-jars on every palace roof.
Though delighted by the attainment of universal sovereignty, the lords of serpents shook their heads, fearing a frown from him;
the king of serpents grieved in vain, for he realized... [the rest of the verse].
Beholding the glory of the night-lotuses that are his enemies, he bestows it upon the lotus-clan of his friends.
Having attained his rise over the circle of the earth, that king became a source of wonder to no one.
In the matter of liberality, let us cite King Karṇa; in statesmanship, Rāma; and in valor, Dhanañjaya.
But in this age of Kali, what example can there be for circles of scholars? 67.

In his kingdom, the Dharma resounded as if it were roaring; the seal of poverty appeared as if it had vanished somewhere; prosperity seemed to have blossomed forth; even the tree of statesmanship flourished as if it were dancing with joy. (68)
For those people who beheld Hamīra, there arose no Kālānala, no Nābhirāma, no Rāma, nor did Bharata become their delight; even Janaka was not present in their hearts. (69)
Those very days were bringers of happiness when King Hammīradeva was born;
those people alone attained auspicious vision who beheld this lotus-like face of his. (70)
Under the guise of the brilliance of her teeth and lips, which were like the fresh sprouts of a blooming white water-lily,
she spread forth from the ocean of the passion for the limbs of his heart these very bright rays as if they were fish.
Then Jaitrasiṃha, afflicted by illness and perceiving his own end to be near, began out of affection to impart this instruction on kingship to King Hammīra. (72)
Do not place your trust anywhere in women or in riches, for they are fragile as a moment;
they may be attached or detached even toward the virtuous, and at every step they quickly lead to misfortune.
O Lord of Men, having attained sovereignty over the greatest of beings, do not forget your humility;
for a man who is undisciplined is like the great sun—a cause of destruction for his entire lineage. (74)
Even while performing noble deeds after due deliberation, this discerning man is beloved by the people of the world;
O Father, how then could this royal fortune, which dwells in the world, ever abandon him? (75)

Even though capable, a person who does not manifest their own power will never attain the state of supreme prosperity; tell me, my child, who would not quickly be overstepped by a fire made of cow-dung? (76)
A king who is always devoted to virtuous conduct should be served even by sages free from desire;
for one who possesses the luster of good character will surely become a source of enjoyment for the wicked, just as oil is for a lamp-wick. //77//
Just as virtue, wealth, and pleasure, or conciliation, bribery, and sowing dissension, were to be employed in succession in former times, so too,
when the practice of these has entirely ceased, the mind should now be fixed upon punishment alone, as it is upon liberation.
That king who is immediately addicted to sense-objects increases the afflictions within his own very self;
when a poisonous tree has been planted within the courtyard of his home, how long can that household remain in a state of well-being? (79)
The five duties of sovereignty are indeed said by the wise here to be the five sense-faculties;
when these dissolve, the sovereignty itself dissolves, just as the body [perishes] when they do. (80)
Having acquired power, a man should always act with vigor and exertion;
indeed, look at the lion—among the many animals—is he not the king of beasts solely through his prowess? (81)
One who possesses wisdom and is properly disciplined and engaged does not fail;
for even a lion, would he enter against an elephant merely by relying on deceit, without any strength at all? || 82 ||
If success is achieved through the Buddha alone, then the ritual of striking with flowers should also be prescribed;
see how Smara, even while fighting with flowers, met his end at the hands of Hara.
Courage and wisdom form a pair; from this untainted dyad, sovereignty arises eternally.
Do not look at the universe as consisting of a single factor alone; everything is produced only from a duality.
Indeed, even one who is powerful and desirous of victory must certainly undertake an expedition against an enemy who is yet to be conquered;
for even a forest fire, though its mass of flames has made the quarters of the sky like matted hair, is not able to burn up the waters.
One who knows the ritual rules should perform the rites of hospitality even for an enemy who has come to one's own abode;
for instance, did not the son of Bhṛgu attain a high station when he reached the portion of Pisces?
O you whose wealth is wisdom, act in such a way that no harm comes to the people;
for does a flower-gatherer pluck flowers while causing injury to the creepers? (87)

Only he by whom they were carried in the womb truly knows, for the most part, the nature of the pleasure and pain of living beings; how much less can a woman who is herself to be slaughtered know the nourishing of the fetus or the exhaustion of carrying it? || 88 ||
If a king seizes wealth from his subjects without regard for their offenses, he does not truly know them as his own;
this is an ill omen for a monarch, for upon the destruction of his kingdom, neither that wealth nor those subjects remain.
Even at the loss of all his possessions, no wise man should ever incite discord within his family.

The enmity created within the family brought Suyodhana to his immediate destruction; what else could it have done? Affliction among the subjects and strife within one's own kin—these two sides act like a grinding machine upon this kingdom.
Like grain reduced to powder, the kingdom lacks the power to sprout again.

Nourishing only himself and deceiving his lord, a group of dependents does not deserve to be neglected; for why is the grass and weeds growing in a field not uprooted when one is drawing the essence from the soil? Like a mother, the king is the benefactor of his subjects, while the class of officials is like a co-wife to that mother.
And when they have been placed in her hand by her, where is there any growth for these [flowers], and where is there life? 93.
A king's dependent, even if of noble birth and superior, must never be overly compliant;
for one who is dull-witted grows like a banyan tree and becomes the cause of the destruction of the royal palace. (94)

Even when being humiliated by his rivals, a wise man does not abandon his own country, aspiring to rise once more; for even though its light is eclipsed by the sun, the moon does not fail to rise again in the sky.
Having abandoned the long-standing and most excellent ministers, the burden of sovereignty was placed upon new ones;
in an instant, it perishes from its very root, just as water does in unbaked jars.
In the counsels of state, it is said that there should indeed be only one excellent minister, and not a second;
for those who know the art of mounting a pair of chariots do not consider it to be a risk to life.
If one is attached to or averse to a particular object, there can be no discernment regarding that object for him;
therefore, a wise person should not provide instruction on the ritual of mantras to such a person.
The wise do not say that even many mantras are more beneficial for numerous companions in wisdom;
for how could they bring welfare to the fetus and its mother, alas, when there are many midwives? (99)

Having first deliberated thoroughly upon the mantra within one's own heart, one should then seek formal approval. If it is confirmed [by the teacher], then this should be performed; if not, one's mind should be withdrawn from it through reasoned reflection.

A man who has previously been treated with contempt should never again be appointed to a position of authority; for having encountered such an occasion for deception, those who harbor secret enmity will surely seek to do him harm. (101)
O wise one, a man who has been offended does not abandon his state of enmity even at the end of an eon;
even today, does Rāhu ever cease from attacking the sun or the moon? || 102 ||
Even one of great strength should not engage in strife with Indra, who possesses brilliant guile;
likewise, though powerful, Bali was conquered by Janārdana, who is preeminent in stratagem.
A game of dice, which keeps one perpetually awake with its ever-increasing intensity, must be abandoned from afar;
for what kind of humiliation did not the sons of Pāṇḍu undergo through the power of their addiction to gambling? 104.

O dear one, he who, having deliberated upon the relative strengths and weaknesses found within the Sūtras, composes a commentary that includes reasoned arguments, alone attains the preeminent status of one who knows the scriptures and is worthy of the profound respect due to various teachers. 105.
Having received this instruction from Dakṣa, regarding auspicious bonds and friendship, and with a mind free from desire for both home and body,
the victorious Lord, desiring his own spiritual welfare, set out toward the city of Śrī Āśrama.

There shines Śivā as well, the caravan leader on the path of knowledge, where the self-existent Śiva himself resides; he who, merely being meditated upon, bestows everything—why not both worldly enjoyment and liberation quickly upon those possessed of great devotion? (107)

There, the river Carmaṇvatī flows with water as dark as collyrium, its banks adorned by twin *akuvalaya* flowers that resemble the eyes of a peacock’s tail; it shines like the braid of the Goddess of Merit.
Then, as he was about to burn, scorched by the fire of separation— as if his lotus-eyes were raining down streams of tears—
the chief ministers approached him from behind, sprinkled him with water from their hearts, and addressed him.

O Lord, although we previously desired liberation, having abandoned the sovereign fortune of empire, now that we are separated from you, our past merits no longer shine forth, like fireflies in the darkness of separation from you. (110)
O Lord of Men, this city shall attain a splendor free from the conjunction of the gaze of those like you,
resembling the beauty of the sky when it is devoid of the rising sun and the blazing orb of the moon.
As if sprinkling them with a gentle glance like a shower of nectar, the king spoke to them:
"Do not inflict this painful misfortune upon us, who are wise, for it was done by me desiring my own welfare."
This city, currently devoid of splendor and lamentable due to the heat of the sun’s fierce rays, will surely before long become exceedingly beautiful when the golden moon has risen. (113)
This king of swans at the lotus-feet of my lineage, whose virtues have earned him praise from the whole world,
shall always gladden you with gifts of grace, just as I do when he is attended upon by you.
Thus, as that lord of men was departing for the city, leaving them behind, a spider emerged from its web and fell; at that very moment, he himself swiftly attained divinity.

Then, for the illustrious Lord Jaitrasiṃha, who was accompanied by his eight beloved and cherished wives—women whom he had never known to suffer separation—the rites of cremation were performed right there by those learned in the ordinances. || 116 ||
Then Hammīradeva, his soul overwhelmed by grief, performed lamentations as he consecrated King Aśoka—the new incarnation [of his father]—with floods of tears in his heart. (117)
O Lord of the Earth, although my throat is parched with grief from crying out "Father!
Father!", you still do not grant me the sight of you; how can this conduct of yours be considered consistent with propriety? 118.
Your hand, which was made submissive to fashion him who acts as the ornament of the entire three worlds—how is it that very same hand now practices audacity for his destruction? O cursed hope! 119.

Who could have fashioned the fire, the wicked man, and the kālakūṭa poison as being equal to King Jaitrasiṃha, the scorcher of his enemies? When [the poet] was about to strike down that king, the Creator provided this answer for him. (120)
O Dhātṛ, although you are not afraid even of the world’s reproach or public censure, alas, how could your hands bear to slay this jewel among men? 121.
I suspect that someone, having taken up hearts as hard as thunderbolts and mountains, fashioned them for the Creator;
for even now, though I cry out thus with a loud voice, they do not restrain themselves out of compassion.
There, for Hamīradeva, the days passed with "Alas! Alas! on his throat, tears from his eyes, the hollow of his lotus-like hands upon his cheeks, and grief in his heart as his only refuge.

Thus, for the benefit of the people, he was rescued from being submerged in this great ocean of sorrow by the most excellent among the knowers of Brahman—Āditya and others—who were like helmsmen for those whose boat of wisdom had been lost. 124.
"My father has met his death"—do not, O protector of the earth, indulge in grief over this in vain.
Have you not seen or heard of all those fathers here who were inevitably destined for death? (125)
Life must indeed have its limit in breath; for breath is well known to be nothing but air.
There is nothing else here more flickering than air, yet that one lives—this is truly a great marvel! 126.
For how long will this swan sport here in the pond of his body, where he is being drawn up by the row of buckets on the water-wheel of Time, while emitting smooth and joyful, sweet notes?
For the water of the peacock dries up instantly because of this. || 127 ||
This is the night of illusion, thick with darkness, created by the playful delusions of ignorance; therefore, O people, remain vigilantly awake here.
Indeed, this thief of Time wanders daily within the worlds to seize the life and wealth of embodied beings, remaining unperceived. 128.
By him, who with bow in hand and a desire for the death of the Lord of Laṅkā, had hurled those various millions of Rākṣasas into the mouth of the Lord of the Ancestors (Yama)—
even that Rāma was suddenly swallowed by Kāla, the night-stalker, whose gaping maw was as terrible as the day and night, his own form fainting in terror.
Your father, who as a child spoke the words of his own mind and as he entered youth uttered such phrases as "Live!"—he who was the very pinnacle of sweetness—where is he now?

Is there the taste of nectar from the moon of the earth in heaven for his pleasure, if his satisfaction is found only in this way through the drinking of the nectar of his own fame sung by the goddesses?

Thus, with his heart delighted by the diversion of traditional wisdom, his disposition awakened by the series of utterances on the specific truths emerging from the lotus-mouth of that sprout of discernment,
he brought forth the heroic faculty of discrimination (*viveka*) in order to utterly crush the army of grief and hatred.
Thereupon, King Hammīra protected the surface of the earth like his own home. || 131 ||

Thus ends the eighth canto, titled "The Description of the Attainment of Sovereignty by the Illustrious King Hammīra," in the great poem *Śrī-Hammīra-Mahākāvya*, marked with the hero, composed by the great poet Śrī-Nayacandrasūri, disciple of the illustrious Jayasiṃhasūri.
Now begins the ninth canto. Then, as he bore the six royal qualities and the three regal splendors,
his mind became yearning for a world-conquest that would be free from obstacles.
Then, at a moment determined by the astrologers to be auspicious, with the sun and planets situated in the ascendant,
he performed the auspicious rites for his journey accompanied by venerable elders of his lineage.
Thereafter, the king—bearing the orb of the sun whose heat had subsided, with his breath drawn upward, and preceded by white splendor—mounted his horse. (A pair of verses.)
Seeing his own extraordinary splendor, the sun, as if thinking, "Let him not suffer from my heat," held a brilliant umbrella over his head with its rays acting as a shade.
Fearing that her entire army would fall under his power,
she approached that boy under the pretext of fanning him, like the Gaṅgā coming to serve him.
Like the lord of Campā from Campā, or Tripura from Tripura,
the steadfast one went out from the city, making the earth tremble.
Like pollen from a lotus, and like arrows from the hand of Pārtha,
the soldiers, their courage flashing before them, marched out behind [the leader].
Muddying the earth on all sides with the waters of their rut,
the elephants went forth, their prowess intimidating the enemies with their thundering roars.
With their wings fiercely flapping and with Puruṣottama mounted upon them,
more than a hundred thousand Garuḍas set forth, appearing like visible Garuḍas themselves.
With excellent chariots bearing rows of lofty banners,
they moved in such a way that the ground was not touched by the sesame seeds scattered within them.
With their faces resonant with loud *huṃkāra* sounds that filled the belly of the sky,
the foot-soldiers, leaping gracefully, gladdened the king's heart.
With their eyes fixed upon the banners overcome by the tossing of the wind, the Vaijayantī flags shone as they called out to one another, "Alas! Alas! (haha).
Although the masses of dust raised by the falling feet of the army were already thick,
they spread out like a canopy in the sky as if for the sake of providing shade for the host.
Some spoke of the kings, some of the foot soldiers, some of the horses, and some of the chariots; none could describe the vastness of his army.
Advancing in due order over the earth with thousands of Gandharvas and hundreds of thousands of foot soldiers,
the steadfast one reached the city of Bhīmarasa.
There, having subdued King Arjuna— who had taken refuge with his enemies—
by striking him with the staff of his sword while roaring, he brought him under the control of his own command.
Then, taking up his hand from the mandala of Durgā, he who was a mass of waters of great splendor swiftly discharged a stream that showered the earth. 17.
There, Bhoja— who was mature in his lineage of supreme enemies and was like another Bhoja—
was made to wither by this king, who was like a lotus.
Then, with the excessive weight of his force, he made the surface of the earth tremble; like a lordly elephant, he made Avanti his forest, its borders smeared with rut.
Seeing the ramparts quickly sprinkled with drops of water offered by the Brahmins with joined palms,
his soldiers became ready for the ritual bath.
There, the elephants—whose bonds were released, who had performed auspicious collyrium rites, and whose hearts were devoted to the service of the Revā river—did not remain [in their stalls]. || 21 ||
Shaking their necks and manes, the horses, having emerged from their bath,
spread a shower [of spray] upon the bank of the river with their brilliant luster.

With her elephant’s temples emerging like rising water-jars, that river, with eyes like those of a cakora bird, swept away the camp of the soldiers, just as a full and swelling breast might overwhelm a small garment.
The king also, having performed his ablutions and with a mind solely intent on giving beneficial gifts,
worshipped Mahākāla there— the destroyer of the enemies that are evil deeds.
Having entered its center and beholding that vast expanse of pure splendor,
he of smiling prowess repeatedly recalled Vikramāditya.
Turning away from there, that leader of the heroic, producing every kind of song held in his own hand, caused Citrakūṭa to resound.
Then, having clearly attained proficiency in the art of shattering the Medapāṭa [kingdom] by means of his dancing,
he reached Mount Arbuda and, possessing dense splendor, established his dwellings there.
There, the elephants, fierce in battle, perceived their own reflections in the crystal rocks through their perceptive intellects, thinking them to be [other] elephants. 28.
There, the shimmering rays of the clusters of emeralds produced in those horses the illusion of the color of fresh dūrvā grass.
With their armies stationed around Adhiśaṅkha,
the kings, along with their armor, shone like great warriors upon the trees of the king of mountains.
Resting there again and again at the foot of tree after tree,
the king heard his own glories being sung by the Bhilla women.
Through the cries of peacocks, which were delighted by those serpents meditated upon with intense concentration,
his fame— originating from the guardians of the directions— seemed to have filled the world like Mount Arbuda.
His mountain streams doubled by the waters from the rut-fluid of the temples of elephants, he ascended the back of that mountain and beheld the pride of his enemy.
In his dwelling, this pure-souled one bowed to the Lord Ṛṣabha, who was himself stainless; for in the minds of the most excellent, there is no conceptualization of self and other.
There, he beheld the glorification of the illustrious Vastupāla, which cuts through the Kali age; struck with wonder, he shook his head many times. (35)
Then, having bowed with great devotion to the Arbuda mountain,
the king rested for a moment in the hermitage of Arundhatī’s husband.
Having performed an extensive ablution in the Mandākinī river, which pacifies all ailments,
she then worshipped Acaleśvara, who is worthy of worship by the entire world.
Having witnessed here the archery of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son, Dhananjaya, in person, the king’s eyes became wide with amazement. (38)
There, the lord of Arbuda, who was an enemy to Maināka— the son of the ocean of swaying creepers—
possessed a pride that surpassed all other lords of mountains.

Then, descending from there, the illustrious one, whose prowess was like that of Viṣṇu, made the city of Vardhana— which had been impoverished— prosperous once more, and he made even the earth, though its Gaṅgā was flowing away, beautiful again.
Making Mount Meru his center,
that knower of duty reached the sacred site of Puṣkara and acquired merit that is difficult to attain.
There the king worshipped Hari, who bears the name Ādivarāha— the wonderful one who, despite possessing ten incarnations, has not undergone the nature of being consumed by fire.
He beheld the mountains, whose caves resounded with the echoes of the sound of the marching drums, appearing as if entirely intent upon singing his own fame.
Then, at the gateway of Śākambharī, the lord of the earth had the entirety of his beauty drunk up by the side-long glances of the courtesans.
I believe that from the tears shed by the eyes of the wives of his enemies,
this salt-mine here was produced in those ancient times.
Thereafter, the king laid waste Mahārāṣṭra, whose sovereign had been destroyed; Khaṇḍuilla, whose splendor was shattered; and Campā, which trembled with intense quaking.
Then, O illustrious one, having made Karālaśrī terrifying for those dwelling here, you, the lord of the mountain of the three worlds, bestowed a great boon upon him as he approached. 47.
Thus, bearing his command like a playful crest-jewel upon the crowns of kings in all four directions, he reached the outskirts of his own city.
Upon the arrival of the king, the ocean of the citizens' passion within the city seemed to overflow,
as if assuming a state of tidal surge under the guise of its swaying red banners.
As the Lord approached, as if out of abundant affection, the city itself seemed to mock him under the guise of the radiant divine garments of the mature women emerging at the gate.
Then, while the Brahmins raised their uplifted hands and offered benedictions, he heard them as the quarters of the sky were made resonant by the shouts of "Victory! from the throngs of bards.

Having approached with his foremost ministers, such as Dharmasiṃha, and having been saluted by them, he entered the city— which was like a jewel of the earth— possessing the splendor of a magnificent festival.
Elevated at every door by the citizens out of a desire for the festival,
the water-pots shone like the breasts born upon the chests of the Goddesses of the mansions.
Then, as if summoned from all sides by the crackling sounds of rows of frying pans,
the women abandoned their other duties and rushed forward to see him.
Having placed one earring on her ear and holding another in her hand,
she shone before him like the army of King Ananga with its discus flashing in front.
With her eyes fixed on the Supreme One, she shone as if saying, "I am capable of conquering the entire universe with a single sidelong glance alone."
Because another [braid] was not yet finished, a braid held by five fingers bore the illusion of a swarm of bees emerging from the interior of a lotus bud.
In the hand of one woman shone a betel-roll half-chewed by teeth;
on her forehead was a dark, thin line, like the crescent of the moon.
Having loosened her untied waist-knot with her very hand,
she set out from the palace like a female elephant with its trunk moving gracefully.
A certain woman, having suddenly snatched her foot from the hand of her hairdresser, stepped forward,
the ground beneath her clearly revealed by the marks of her ornaments.
A certain woman, fearing that her own breasts had been stolen by the elephant-like temples of the eyes of the god whose complexion is known to be like a lotus,
repeatedly searched her own chest with her hand. (69)
The supreme goddess, adorning her left limb, bears [the other] upon her right limb.
We say that there is a mutual equality between these two alone, who have both conquered the universe.
Behold another woman, who has raised her neck and whose feet are pressed against the ground;
she appears as if she were the frontal lobes of an elephant, rising up with her breasts elevated to conquer them.
In the braided hair of a certain woman, a flower bud emerged between her fingers;
surrounded by rows of petals, it shone like a campaka blossom.
Holding a golden necklace upon her lotus-like hand,
she shone as if she were a snare intended to ensnare the deer-like eyes of young men.
With her left foot well-adorned by tinkling anklets,
she further kindled the passion of those who were already enamored with the beauty of Ardhanārīśvara.
The protective amulet placed upon the head of another woman, resting at the end of her braid,
shone like the jewel on the hood of a serpent during the expansion of its hood.
Making the waist slender and bringing heaviness to the breasts,
the upper body of women shone as if it had taken refuge in sovereign power.
As she drank from this shoreless ocean of loveliness with her two eyes, the women, who had already drunk the ocean with its shores using their three moving [eyes], were surpassed by her.
Having found their opportunity, some pierced the king with side-long glances;
Kāma, as if he were an archer, then struck him with his arrows.
Drinking the nectar of the king's beauty, they found no satiety;
nevertheless, some immediately began to shake their heads. (71)
Thus, his beauty being drunk in by the side-glances of the beautiful women of the city, he reached his own palace.
With his vast prowess having overwhelmed the earth and bringing destruction to those who acted against him,
there was no Janārdana anywhere who remained unshakable in his station.
In the great poem *Śrīhammīra*, these three human goals known as dharma, artha, and kāma—
having attained their respective opportunities— attended upon him in due course. (74)
Bearing the majesty of non-violence and shining with every auspiciousness, even Maheśvara was not despondent in that kingdom; indeed, such a person was extraordinary.
When the king asked about the fruit of ten million sacrifices, the skillful family priest,
known by the name Viśvarūpa, explained it to him as follows.

Having conquered the earth by the strength of his arms and performing the Koṭihoma sacrifice as prescribed, a king who is thus engaged shall become an object of affection for the glories of the celestial realm.
Having heard those words of his, which shone like a flash from the spray of the ocean of the nectar of the Smṛtis, the king desired to perform that sacrifice.
Then, summoned by Indra, who was delighted with the earth, the Brahmins gathered there—
those who were like submarine fires to the ocean of evil deeds.
The streaks of Gopīcandana upon the limbs of the Brahmins shone like waves from the ocean of nectar of the four Vedas surging within them. (80)
Because of their constant bathing, their hair had become tawny,
as if from within it they were bearing a supreme splendor upon their heads.
Their hands were adorned by rosaries of rudrākṣa beads cast about by their double-twirling movements, as if by bees settled there in the mistaken belief that they were lotuses.
[He was seen] by great sages who dispel the fear of the mass of sins, who illuminate auspicious dwellings, and who shower down supreme bliss.
At that time, three special wonders occurred in the city: the warding off of Māra, the avoidance of the seven calamities, and the liberation of those who were imprisoned. 84.
There the altar shone, with its arched gateways as creeper-like eyebrows and its lofty auspicious jars as breasts, appearing like the Goddess of Sacrifice incarnate.
Under the guise of the smoke from the sacrificial oblations, he scattered away the sins of the enemy;
here the flame of his tongue blazed forth, its flickering tongues churning the very sky.
The Description of Hammīra’s Sacrifice:
At the command of the twice-born, the king, his gaze fixed upon the sacrificial initiation, took up residence by the side of the altar after having mastered the Upaniṣads. (87)
The thirty-three crores of demons summoned by mantras offered a circle of substances into the great fire, like submarine fires.
By means of that pure luster, the abundant successions of clarified butter offered by the Brahmins were made to overflow through the power of the Vedic mantras. (89)

Because they were intent on that purpose, the gods, as if terrified by the fear of being consumed by the flames due to the pouring of that nectar, accepted the oblations even as they were falling toward them. (90)
While the Vedic priests joyfully chanted the Rigvedic verses in sweet tones, the sacrificial fire seemed to dance under the guise of its flickering rows of flames. 99.
O lords of the twice-born, by the power of the king’s merit, they proceeded without obstacle to the completion of the sacrificial rites, just as ascetics reach the further shore of existence.

Then the god among men gave ten million gold pieces and the earth of inexhaustible wealth to the gods upon earth (the Brahmins), as well as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) endowed with beautiful characteristics.
Beholding the twice-born dancing upon the heaps of gold bestowed by the king, the gods recognized their own pride in sporting on the lap of Mount Meru;
they thought, "In this world, he has likewise gratified his supplicants with gifts of gold."
Leaving them aside, she approached the donor with great height, according to her desire.
Some praised the illustrious Hammīra as the bestower of heaps of jewels, some as the giver of abundant gold coins, and others as the giver of elephants and horses. 96.
Bestowing gifts that transcend thought, imagination, and desire, he felt disdain for the wish-fulfilling gem, the celestial kalpa-tree, and the vessel of plenty.
Then, with great joy, the king prepared an abundant feast for the twice-born, exquisite with the flavors of milk and other delicacies mixed with sugar and candied sugar.
Then, urged by his domestic priest, the king, being pleased, accepted the worthy priest who had undertaken the single vow of a sage. (99)
In this great poem on Hammīra, there appeared here a preeminent Śaka named Allāvadīna, who was the foremost among the brave and who struck down the enemies of his foes. (100)
Then, having assumed the form of King Jñāta, he who was the sole conqueror of the world addressed his own brother, who was known by the name Ulchūkhāna.
In ancient times, Jaitrasiṃha was the sovereign of Raṇastaṃbhapura;
out of fear of my fierce power, he always paid me tribute. (102)
His son, named Hammīra, now possesses immense pride;
let alone punishment, he does not even grant a word from afar. (106)
Because of his great power, he could not be conquered for a long time;
yet now, through the power of her vows on this lunar day, he is being defeated with ease.
Having gone there to that region of the base of the pillar of Araṇa for its destruction, once the region is destroyed, how many days could he, even if powerful, endure to remain? (105)
Having thus received the command of his lord, the intolerant Ulūka set out with great speed,
accompanied by a vast force of cavalry and possessing immense prowess.
His army-ocean shone forth, with galloping horses as its surging waves, trumpeting elephants as its thundering clouds,
and weapons honed on whetstones as its submarine fire.
Bent by the weight of his own strength and unable to enter the interior due to the expansion of Vāsuki’s hoods, he remained on the shore of the ocean.
Setting fire to deserted villages and driving about cattle with wet fodder,
he passed the remaining eighteen days in comfort.
While the king remained silent, having undertaken his vows with triple purity, the commander-in-chief Bhīmasiṃha, who was preeminent in his devotion to King Dharmasiṃha, [acted]. || 110 ||
Taking with him an army crowded with excellent heroes who were leaping and brandishing weapons in battle, the one of great heroism advanced toward the enemy force. 111.
Hearing the sounds of the drums being beaten and the blasts of the trumpets,
the Śakas fell into a state of agitation within their camp.
Some fierce warriors hurled sharp javelins at the elephants in battle, while others,
with uplifted enthusiasm, swiftly re-saddled their mounts.
Some did not take up their quivers even though they were unfastened; some did not grasp their mallets; some did not draw their swords; and no one indeed took up their shields. || 114 ||
By the falling of fierce blows, some played musical instruments to inform the warriors and to urge them to assemble quickly for battle. || 115 ||
Bestowing courage upon his troops,
the leader Nayollūkha himself went forth, mounting a sea-elephant with the prowess of the ocean.
Under the guise of dark and white chowries hanging from the tips of the bamboo poles,
the sky appeared as if marked by the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
Then, from their mutual glances,
a great enmity arose between the Ākānas and the Bāhujas, like that between the Daityas and the gods.
Foot-soldier against foot-soldier, rider against rider, charioteer against charioteer, and horseman against horseman— the soldiers thus challenged one another.
"Lest there be an interruption of the essence of our battle through this scorching heat," as if thinking thus, the warriors first spread a pavilion of arrows across the sky.
Touching their limbs, the enemy’s arrows brought joy to the heroic elephants, just as the side-long glances of beautiful women bring pleasure to lovers. || 999 ||
The heroes, with arrows shot by their enemies lodged in all their limbs,
shone as if possessed of horripilation from the joy of embracing the Goddess of Victory.
When a canopy of clouds was fashioned by arrows spreading without interruption,
it was only natural that the swans flew up from the heart-lakes of living beings.
Having made their arrows whirl within the lotus-faces of their enemies,
they struck down their hearts and drank the essence of their lives.
Whose heart would not have rejoiced at the clashing sounds of sword-blades amidst the millions of heroes dancing with joy upon the field of battle? 125.
In the great poem *Śrīhammīra*, millions of warriors attained a divine mode of existence by means of their transient lives, through the acquisition of imperishable fame. 126.
Leaping again and again, desiring to sever the heads of their riders,
those warriors shone as if they were alive even while seeking to reach heaven.
The swords of the heroes, reddened by blood, shone in battle like the flickering tongues of fire consuming the flesh of the man-eaters. 128.
Reaching even the mere touch of the soldiers, they sent them into the belly of Yama;
thus, the name "Yamadaṃṣṭra" (Yama’s Tusk), which was their own, attained its true meaning.
Even on the battlefield, which was jagged with heads falling, severed by swords,
the heroes did not stumble as they ran, as if supported by their own valor.
"Today in battle, the elephant has destroyed the frontal globes of your pride," saying this,
some men licked the tusks of the elephants with their tongues for the sake of the women's understanding.
Seeing the sons of the Bahikas who had reached equal ground,
the Yavanas became agitated and placed their heroic elephants at the front.
Their chests filled with arrows that pierced their vital organs,
the enemy elephants stood with their trunks raised, as if paralyzed.
Then, how can the battle of those preeminent warriors be described, when even their scriptures fought one another under the guise of mutual impact? (134)
As they traveled along the great road, clouds of dust rose up;
they could recognize one another only by their respective languages.
Thus it flashed forth in that battle where the messengers of Death were being gratified; the Cāhamānas crushed the enemy force like grain being ground.
Out of fear of the enemy, the soldiers protected the people who had entered their bodies as headless trunks;
even when they themselves were killed, they did not abandon their vow of providing refuge.
With parasols cast down from the hands of soldiers who had fallen under the heat of intense distress,
even the earth appeared as if it were eager for battle.
Placing their feet upon the tusks of elephants and striking out,
the riders caused the hearts of both horsemen and chariot-warriors to falter. (139)
There were none among them who were not horsemen, none who were not riders, and none who were not warriors—
none who were not filled to the breast with the arrows of Cāhamāna.
Some [abandoned] horses, some elephants, some weapons, and others their chariots;
crying out "Alas! Alas!", the Śakas, struck by the divine weapon, perished like crows.
Some held grass in their mouths, while others fell at his feet; some cried out, "He is your cow," and others, speaking like Śakas, said, "Save our lives! (142)
Having thus addressed Śatānīka, Bhīmasiṃha turned back;
the indignant Ullūkhāna also followed him in secret. (143)
The Bāhuja warriors, having stripped away many crores of golden armors and breastplates,
abandoned Bhīma from behind and went forward, exulting in their victory.
Entering the unobstructed [palace], even the formidable lion, with supreme joy,
tore away and loudly sounded the musical instruments seized from the Śakas.
Wherever the sound of one's own musical instruments spreads far and wide,
there everyone should go, considering it a victory.
Thus, deluded by this signal and imagining victory for themselves,
the Yavanas then rushed forward with speed, perceiving that appearance as the actual object.
Seeing his own army assembled, Śakra advanced to fight;
Bhīmasiṃha also marched forth—for how could such as he be cowards? (148)
Having fought a great battle there and slain more than a hundred Śakas,
Bhīmasiṃha perished, his entire body shattered by arrows.
Even Śakra, appearing victorious, upon reaching the camp, cried out loudly and,
fearing the kṣatriyas once more, retreated toward his own city.
Then King Pūrṇavrata, thinking that Dharmasiṃha had abandoned the mountain-ridges through his intellect and that Bhīmasiṃha had arrived, challenged him.
In the great poem of Śrī Hammīra, your eyes have surely burst open, since the powerful Śaka was not seen;
that you yourself stood last is proof that even your manliness has departed from you. (252)
Having reproached him with insults and censured him repeatedly in the presence of the assembly, the king first caused his two eyes to be gouged out by means of a pair of testicles.
Like Vidura was born to that King Paṇḍu a victorious younger brother named Bhojadeva, who bore the other name Khaḍgagrāhin (the Sword-bearer). 154.
Then the king, being pleased, bestowed upon him the title of Dharmasiṃha;
and as he was about to banish him from the country, he was restrained by this very [Dharmasiṃha].
Then, having returned to his own palace after that insult, he harbored a secret enmity;
while studying the Bharata, he taught the Goddess Dhārā the art of dancing.
And that king, although remaining at home, learned of the entire state of affairs in the royal assembly through his maidservant, who reported it incessantly under the guise of dancing.
On another day, her body withered by anxiety, she arrived at the king's assembly;
questioned by the blind man, she spoke of the cause of her grief, which was tearing her heart asunder.
"Father, today my mother died from the disease of piercing (vedha) upon hearing of the Lord;
for his pleasure, there was no singing, dancing, or the like, and because of that, this intense grief has arisen. (159)
Having heard this, he said to her: "Do not prepare this funeral pyre in vain;
rather, you should request the king when the opportunity arises. (160)
O Lord, O Lion of Dharma, if one attains your own state again, he shall bring back from the dead twice as many horses as there were before. 161.
Having agreed, saying "Om," she went and reported this to the king;
out of greed, he summoned that base man and reinstated him in his own position.
The lamp of discernment shall shine in the hearts of the virtuous as long as it does not succumb to madness from the wind of the fever of craving.
This strange creeper of craving appears ever new; it is not good that the sharp axe of true discernment should suffer dullness against it.
Even a mere drop [of power],
when blinded by the intoxication of flickering greed,
causes one to treat enemies as brothers and brothers as enemies. (165)
Then, desiring to act out of indignation and wishing to retaliate for his enmity,
he made long-range plans to destroy that kingdom.
Having made King Lobhadṛṣṭi his instrument for the seizure of wealth, he oppressed the subjects by inflicting cruel punishments. || 167 ||
Seizing horses from those who possessed horses and wealth from those who were wealthy, that man of cruel deeds became like the time of universal destruction for the worlds. (168)
Filling the treasury with wealth, he became very dear to the king;
for one who bestows wealth is always beloved by both courtesans and kings. (169)
Is that which is diligently and extensively increased by the staff of wisdom for the sake of augmenting one's treasury not rather the nourishment of one's own body with its own flesh? (170)
Then, because he was destined to enjoy his own position, he harbored a long-standing enmity in his heart;
after the completion of the year of enjoyment, he requested from Bhoja the purification of his income.
Then Bhojadeva, seeing the half-appearance [of the head] while enraged, went quickly and addressed the king with his head bowed and palms joined in reverence. (172)
"O King, if you have need of my life, then take it;
however, I cannot endure the torment of the words of one who is utterly ignorant. (173)
The king declared: "The teaching of Dharmasiṃha, for whom there is imperishable devotion toward me, shall not be subverted here by anyone. (174)
Like a master, he is honored by his masters and served by his dependents; is an ox not worshipped for making its steady standing post so firm? 175.
Having recognized that the king was evil-minded by this speech and by the fierce look with which he gazed at his wife, that pure-minded Bhojadeva [acted]. (176)
Like one whose mind is free from effort, he gave away even his entire possession;
for when a task has failed from its very root, what can even a powerful person do? || 177 ||
Thus, in the great poem *Śrī-Hammīra*, there is a pair [of verses]; nevertheless, because of his noble birth, he did not abandon his devotion to his lord.
Like a yogi serving the Supreme Brahman, Bhoja attended upon the king.
The king, having set out on a pilgrimage to Vaijanātha, saw Bhoja standing behind him and spoke these words with indignation: || 179 ||
Indeed, at every single step here, there are many small birds in great abundance;

yet nowhere else is there another so contemptible as this wretched crow. O you who are possessed by anger, read this: though his mass of feathers was being torn away by millions of wounds from the tips of the beaks of a swarm of owls, he did not even leave the edge of the tree, let alone fly away. (180)
Having returned home from the lake with this *Anyokti-kaumudī*, which was like a lotus, Bhoja went to his brother Pīṭhasiṃha in private and spoke to him. (181)
Seeing that he was as good as dead, he became dejected by our words;
even though we were intent on serving him, he did not value us even as much as blades of grass.
Or perhaps kings, whose minds are deluded by the intoxication of having attained immeasurable sovereignty, are never truly devoted to solitude. (183)
"Let us go abroad for a few days under the pretext of a journey;
for those learned in statecraft have declared that when times are inauspicious, the passing of time is beneficial. (184)
Having consulted thus with his uterine brother, he went to the king and petitioned him:
"If the monarch commands, I shall go on a pilgrimage to Kāśī. (185)
The king said: "Are you not going further and further away?
Even without you, will this city not shine as it did before? (186)
Thus, though reviled by the princess, the king maintained his forbearance and set out for Kāṃśī with his retinue, followed by his resentment.

When he had departed, the lord of the earth, his joy overflowing, consecrated Ratipālavīra in the position of *daṇḍanāyaka* through proper means; and he spent his days with intense delight in the pursuit of the three aims of life (*trivarga*), which bring about the singular welfare of the world.

Thus ends the ninth canto, titled "The Description of King Hammīra’s World Conquest," in the great poem *Śrī-Hammīra-mahākāvya*, marked by the hero, composed by the great poet Śrī-Nayacandrasūri, disciple of Śrī-Jayasimhasūri.
Now begins the tenth canto.
Having been insulted by Dharaṇīramaṇa, Bhoja returned with his head held high;
repeatedly reflecting upon his own misfortune, he thought thus in his heart out of pride: ||9||
If the lord of men has inflicted such humiliation upon me without any cause, what other recourse remains for those who possess self-respect if they do not retaliate? (2)
Even a man endowed with virtues, if he has become crooked, is as terrifying as a bow;
for from him, like arrows released from the string by wicked men, extreme suffering is spread abroad. (3)
Even when a person intent on insulting him resorts solely to tranquility, it is better that even a single awn of a grain of millet, being struck at that time, should pierce his foot. (4)
It is said that there is no sin in killing even one's own brothers if they are intent on doing harm;
this is the eternal rule of conduct proclaimed for those possessed of pride who are set upon the path of policy.
The testing of friends or even of enemies is accomplished through their very actions:
for even a friend may prove harmful, while an enemy may prove helpful; thus, one who acts as a friend is a friend, and one who acts as an enemy is an enemy.
If one who is even slightly cowardly in mind endures the defeat wrought by an enemy,
let his mother never again give birth to him, for she would be disgraced by the pride she took in his youth.
Then, after taking leave of his uterine brother Pithama— who was like a temple of noble intellect—
he went to Laghu-yoginīpura and met the lord of the Yavanas.
Even though Bhojadeva was of such noble lineage, that he has now acted in this manner is merely the manifestation of the barbarian;
therefore, even his dust is not fit to settle upon the virtuous.
Then, his soul overcome with joy at that meeting, King Allāvadīna first bestowed upon him gifts of clothing and then gave him that city of Jagarā, the capital of Mudgaleśa.
There, O Bhoja, he who possessed diverse tastes abandoned his own brother, who was free from pride, and returning quickly to Dillī himself, served the leader of the Śakas alone. (11)
In the great poem *Śrī-Hammīra*,
that king likewise nourished him with gifts of beautiful horses, gold, and other riches, which were as vast as the ocean and capable of dispelling great pride, so that he became like his own son. 12.
That Śakra himself quickly rendered even that adversary [Indra] as he deserved;
otherwise, how could he have proclaimed this infallible means for conquering his enemies throughout the world?
Having attained that supreme self, he goes elsewhere; having understood this, the Moon of the Yavanas asked:
"O son of Bhṛgu, tell me, how can this Hammīra be quickly conquered by me in battle? (14)
"It is true, if you ask me; however, O Lord of Mountains, my anger shall not be directed toward our task.
Having spoken these words, the Bhoja king, having laid down his burden, then proceeded fearlessly.
Violently inducing looseness in her tresses, pressing upon her waist, causing her girdle to fall from its place, and increasing the playful grace in her limbs—
he spreads the fortune and splendor of good luck for this woman with steady eyes, like a husband to the Earth.
How could that heroic Śrī Hammīra be conquered in the field of battle, even in play? || 16 ||

When the intense majesty of that moon of the earth spreads most extensively over the surface of the world, the lamp remains only as its wick, glowing with the brilliance of a shimmering red gem; the sun remains only in form, reduced to a mere name; and the row of flames at the edge of the world-destroying fire remains only as a faint glimmer.
How could that heroic Śrī Hammīra be conquered in the field of battle, even by mere play? || 17 ||

In whom the six seasons, like virtues, took up their eternal residence as if in the year— the lord of the earth— and even his powers remained dependent upon him, just as the *guṇas* depend upon the Supreme Puruṣa;
whose army, swelling with its constituent parts as prescribed, manifested his proficiency just as knowledge does.
How could that heroic Śrī Hammīra be conquered in the field of battle, even in play? || 98 ||
Upon seeing whom, even though his hand was skilled at grasping a sword, the kings were so terrified that they had neither breath,
nor staffs, nor a stainless lineage, nor valor, nor fortitude; instead,
they all quickly resorted to flight alone, taking to the path of meditation.
How could that heroic Śrī Hammīra be conquered with ease on the field of battle? || 19 ||

How can that illustrious hero Hammīra—the elder brother of Vīrama, the crest-jewel of the multitude of heroes and conqueror of the world—be defeated with ease on the battlefield? He whose hand, itching for the sport of cleaving the frontal globes of elephants, draws swarms of humming bees attracted by the wafting fragrance of rut flowing from them without fatigue. (20)

Even those northerners— who, because of their clearly manifest prowess as great warriors, considered you not even as a blade of grass, since they unhesitatingly uprooted the pride of your brother whose mind was dense with the pursuit of wealth—
now perform service for him, O King Mahimāsāhi, who is the foremost among the great.
O illustrious hero Hammīra! How could he be conquered in the field of battle even with ease? || 21 ||
That country, whose regions are ever made beautiful by the conduct of people who perform virtuous deeds, is a fortress that cannot be grasped even in thought by the hosts of hostile kings;
therein, the best of heroes, though possessing pure fame won through mutual rivalry of valor, meet in battle.
How could that heroic Śrī Hammīra be conquered in the field of battle except by mere play? || 22 ||
Aṅga does not bear [the weight of] limbs, nor does Kaliṅga assume the marks of battle; Kāśmīra does not carry a smiling face, nor does Vaṅga extend his association with valor;
the Lord of Gurjara makes no roar—yet before the tip of whose sword the one of vast intellect spreads [his fame].
How could that heroic Śrī Hammīra be conquered in the field of battle, even in play? || 23 ||

Before whom not even a blade of grass exists; whose throat is parched with fear at the mere sight of him; whom the Lord of Horses (Uccaiḥśravas), renowned for his wretched intellect, constantly pleads for protection from death;
and whom the Lord of Elephants (Airāvata) mutters mantras for his own safety when caught in the range of his sidelong glance.
How could that heroic Śrī Hammīra be defeated in the field of battle, even in play? || 24 ||
There is someone who is a hero, someone who is wise, someone who is courteous, someone who is learned, and yet another who is virtuous and a donor; thus,
many people exist whose greatness is rooted in the cultivation of each of these individual qualities.
The heroic Hammīra, whose body was presided over by all the most excellent virtues, was supreme.
"O Lord, by the grace of your uplifted lotus-hands, even those who are afflicted by defects attain prosperity; do not consider this to be extraordinary.
Do wish-fulfilling gems (cintāmaṇi) not shine? And are not the udders of the wish-granting cow (kāmadhenu)? Consider it thus."
Are not his fingers the sprouts of the wish-fulfilling trees? 26.
